item.title: Is the Sea Rising at Piraeus? Sea Level in Greece, the Mediterranean and the World
item.description: The tide gauges of the Greek harbours since 1969 and the satellites since 1993: how much the sea has risen at Piraeus, how Greece compares with the Mediterranean and the world, why the land matters, and whether the rise is speeding up.
item.content:encoded:
The tide gauges of the Greek harbours since 1969 and the satellites since 1993: how much the sea has risen at Piraeus, how Greece compares with the Mediterranean and the world, why the land matters, and whether the rise is speeding up.

What is this?

The sea rises as the world warms: water expands as it gets warmer, and the melting glaciers and ice sheets of the land pour more of it into the oceans. This story asks what that means for Greece, a country of more than 13,000 kilometres of coast, with six questions:

  1. How is the height of the sea measured?
  2. Is the sea rising at Piraeus?
  3. How does Piraeus compare with the Mediterranean and the world?
  4. Is the sea rising everywhere in Greece?
  5. Is the rise speeding up?
  6. How much higher could the sea be by 2100?

The data come from the Permanent Service for Mean Sea Level (PSMSL), which keeps the records of the tide gauges of the world, and from the Laboratory for Satellite Altimetry of NOAA, the weather and oceans agency of the United States. Both are downloaded when the page is rendered.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages("plotly")
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# the lines of a file on the web, tried again a few times: the servers sometimes refuse a connection
# or take too long to answer
read_lines<-function(url,tries=4) {
  for(k in seq_len(tries)) {
    result<-tryCatch(readLines(url,warn=FALSE),error=function(e) NULL)
    if(!is.null(result))
      return(result)
    Sys.sleep(10)
  }
  stop("Could not download ",url)
}
# a tide gauge of the PSMSL: the mean sea level of every month, in millimetres above a fixed mark of
# the gauge. Missing months are -99999; months that the PSMSL flags for attention are left out
gauge_months<-function(id) {
  url<-paste0("https://psmsl.org/data/obtaining/rlr.monthly.data/",id,".rlrdata")
  x<-read.table(text=read_lines(url),sep=";",strip.white=TRUE,
                col.names=c("time","mm","missing_days","flags"),
                colClasses=c("numeric","numeric","integer","character"))
  result<-x[x$mm>-99999&x$flags=="000",]
  result$year<-floor(result$time)
  return(result)
}
# the mean of every year with at least ten good months
gauge_years<-function(months) {
  if(nrow(months)==0)
    return(data.frame(year=integer(0),mm=numeric(0)))
  counts<-table(months$year)
  result<-aggregate(mm~year,months,mean)
  result<-result[counts[as.character(result$year)]>=10,]
  return(result)
}
# the rise of a straight line through the yearly means, mm a year
rise<-function(x,from=-Inf,to=Inf) {
  x<-x[x$year>=from&x$year<=to,]
  result<-unname(coef(lm(mm~year,x))[2])
  return(result)
}
# the tide gauges of Greece have long gaps in the 1990s, and Piraeus has doubtful years then (1990
# is flagged), so the recent rise is measured from 2000, when the records run without gaps again
from<-2000
# Piraeus, the port of Athens: PSMSL station 374
piraeus_months<-gauge_months(374)
piraeus<-gauge_years(piraeus_months)
flagged_1990<-!any(piraeus_months$year==1990)
# all the tide gauges of Greece (PSMSL coastline 290), where they are, and their yearly means
station_list<-read_lines("https://psmsl.org/data/obtaining/rlr.monthly.data/filelist.txt")
stations<-read.table(text=station_list,sep=";",strip.white=TRUE,quote="",
                     col.names=c("id","lat","lon","name","coastline","code","flag"))
stations<-stations[stations$coastline==290,]
greek_years<-lapply(stations$id,function(id) gauge_years(gauge_months(id)))
# the gauges with at least 15 yearly means since 2000, and the rise of each since then
recent_years<-sapply(greek_years,function(x) sum(x$year>=from))
long_enough<-recent_years>=15
gauge_rates<-sapply(greek_years[long_enough],function(x) rise(x,from=from))
# how much higher the sea at Piraeus stood in its last ten years than in 1969-1988, cm
recent_piraeus<-piraeus$mm[piraeus$year>max(piraeus$year)-10]
climb<-(mean(recent_piraeus)-mean(piraeus$mm[piraeus$year<=1988]))/10
# NOAA's satellite record of the mean sea level since the end of 1992, with the seasons taken out,
# mm: a column for each satellite, a row for each pass over the ocean
altimetry<-function(region) {
  url<-paste0("https://www.star.nesdis.noaa.gov/socd/lsa/SeaLevelRise/slr/slr_sla_",region,
              "_free_ref_90.csv")
  x<-read.csv(text=read_lines(url),comment.char="#")
  passes<-rowSums(!is.na(x[-1]))>0
  result<-data.frame(time=x$year[passes],mm=rowSums(x[passes,-1],na.rm=TRUE))
  result$year<-floor(result$time)
  return(result)
}
world_passes<-altimetry("gbl")
mediterranean_passes<-altimetry("mds")
# the mean of every year that the satellites saw from beginning to end
satellite_years<-function(passes) {
  span<-tapply(passes$time,passes$year,function(t) max(t)-min(t))
  result<-aggregate(mm~year,passes,mean)
  result<-result[span[as.character(result$year)]>0.9,]
  return(result)
}
world<-satellite_years(world_passes)
mediterranean<-satellite_years(mediterranean_passes)
last_satellite<-max(world$year)
# the rise since 2000 at Piraeus, in the Mediterranean and in the world, over the same years
rates<-c(Piraeus=rise(piraeus,from,last_satellite),Mediterranean=rise(mediterranean,from),
         World=rise(world,from))
# a comparison in words: "faster than", "about as fast as" or "slower than"
compared<-function(a,b) {
  result<-if(abs(a-b)<0.5) "about as fast as" else if(a>b) "faster than" else "slower than"
  return(result)
}
# the same for two amounts: "more than", "about the same as" or "less than"
compared_amount<-function(a,b) {
  result<-if(abs(a-b)<0.5) "about the same as" else if(a>b) "more than" else "less than"
  return(result)
}
Code 
greek_red<-"#d62728"
blue<-"#1f77b4"
gray<-"#9e9e9e"
dark_gray<-"#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes and the labels
# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(),
                margin=list(t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.16,...) {
  note<-list(text=paste("Source:",source),xref="paper",yref="paper",x=0,y=note_y,xanchor="left",
             yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=11,color=dark_gray))
  result<-layout(p,
                 title=list(text=title,x=0.02,xanchor="left",y=0.97,yanchor="top"),
                 yaxis=c(list(title=y_title),y_axis),
                 xaxis=c(list(title=""),x_axis),
                 margin=margin,
                 annotations=c(annotations,list(note)),
                 ...) %>%
    config(displaylogo=FALSE)
  return(result)
}
legend_top<-list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.02,yanchor="bottom")
# yearly means in centimetres above their own average of 2000-2019, so that a tide gauge and the
# satellites can share a chart
rebase<-function(x) {
  result<-data.frame(year=x$year,cm=(x$mm-mean(x$mm[x$year>=2000&x$year<=2019]))/10)
  return(result)
}
# every year from the first to the last, with NA where a year is missing, so the line breaks there
all_years<-function(x) {
  result<-merge(data.frame(year=min(x$year):max(x$year)),x,all.x=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
# short labels of numbers
mm_year<-function(x) {
  result<-paste0(format(round(x,1),nsmall=1,trim=TRUE)," mm a year")
  return(result)
}

1. How is the height of the sea measured?

With tide gauges since the 19th century, and with satellites since 1992. A tide gauge sits in a harbour and measures the height of the water against a fixed mark on land, every few minutes; the average of a month or a year smooths out the tides, the waves and the weather. Since the end of 1992 satellites have also measured the height of the whole ocean, by timing a radar pulse from the satellite to the sea and back.

The two measure different things. A satellite measures the sea against the centre of the Earth. A tide gauge measures the sea against the land it stands on, and in Greece the land moves: earthquakes lift it or drop it, and soft ground under some cities sinks. For the people of a harbour, the tide gauge measures what matters.

2. Is the sea rising at Piraeus?

Yes, since about 2000; before that it hardly rose at all. The tide gauge of Piraeus has measured the sea since 1969. From 1969 to 1988, when its record runs with few gaps, a straight line through its yearly means falls by 0.8 mm a year. From 2000 to 2025 it rises by 3.3 mm a year. The years in between are left out of both lines: several are missing, and some look doubtful (the PSMSL flags all the months of 1990, as the weather of that year disturbed the gauge). In all, the sea at Piraeus stood 2.9 cm higher in 2016–2025 than in 1969–1988.

Code 
cm<-all_years(rebase(piraeus))
before<-cm[!is.na(cm$cm)&cm$year<=1988,]
after<-cm[!is.na(cm$cm)&cm$year>=from,]
fit_before<-fitted(lm(cm~year,before))
fit_after<-fitted(lm(cm~year,after))
plot_ly(cm,x=~year,y=~cm,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers",name="Yearly mean",
        line=list(color=gray,width=1.5),marker=list(color=gray,size=6),
        hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} cm<extra></extra>") %>%
  add_trace(x=before$year,y=fit_before,mode="lines",name=paste0("Trend ",min(before$year),"–1988"),
            line=list(color=blue,width=3),hoverinfo="skip",inherit=FALSE,type="scatter") %>%
  add_trace(x=after$year,y=fit_after,mode="lines",name=paste0("Trend since ",from),
            line=list(color=greek_red,width=3),hoverinfo="skip",inherit=FALSE,
            type="scatter") %>%
  chart("Sea level at Piraeus, cm",
        paste0("PSMSL, station 374, yearly means, ",min(piraeus$year),"–",max(piraeus$year),
               ": flagged months and years of fewer than ten months left out"),
        "cm above the average of 2000–2019",legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90))

Interactive chart: Sea level at Piraeus, cm

3. How does Piraeus compare with the Mediterranean and the world?

Since 2000 the sea at Piraeus has risen about as fast as the Mediterranean as a whole and the world’s oceans. Straight lines through the yearly means of 2000–2024:

Code 
knitr::kable(data.frame(sea=c("Piraeus (tide gauge)","Mediterranean (satellites)",
                              "World (satellites)"),
                        rate=mm_year(rates)),
             col.names=c("Sea",paste0("Rise, ",from,"–",last_satellite)),align="lr")
Sea Rise, 2000–2024
Piraeus (tide gauge) 3.3 mm a year
Mediterranean (satellites) 2.9 mm a year
World (satellites) 3.6 mm a year
Code 
series<-list(Piraeus=rebase(piraeus[piraeus$year>=from,]),
             Mediterranean=rebase(mediterranean[mediterranean$year>=from,]),
             World=rebase(world[world$year>=from,]))
colors<-c(Piraeus=greek_red,Mediterranean=blue,World=dark_gray)
p<-plot_ly()
for(name in names(series)) {
  p<-p %>%
    add_trace(data=all_years(series[[name]]),x=~year,y=~cm,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers",
              name=name,line=list(color=colors[[name]],width=2),
              marker=list(color=colors[[name]],size=6),
              hovertemplate=paste0(name,": %{y:.1f} cm<extra></extra>"))
}
p %>%
  chart(paste0("Sea level since ",from,", cm"),
        paste("PSMSL, station 374; NOAA Laboratory for Satellite Altimetry (seasons removed).",
              "Each against its average of 2000–2019."),
        "cm above the average of 2000–2019",hovermode="x unified",legend=legend_top,
        margin=list(t=100,b=110),note_y=-0.2)

Interactive chart: Sea level since 2000, cm

A single harbour moves up and down more from year to year than the average of a whole sea, with the winds, the air pressure and the currents of each year; that is why Piraeus zigzags around the smoother lines of the satellites. And the tide gauge measures the sea against the land: the land of Piraeus seems to have moved little.

4. Is the sea rising everywhere in Greece?

At every harbour with a long enough record, but not equally, because the land moves too. Every tide gauge of Greece with at least 15 yearly means since 2000:

Code 
# common English names of the harbours, for the PSMSL's transliterations
english<-c(PIRAIEVS="Piraeus",KHIOS="Chios",POSIDHONIA="Posidonia",SOUDHAS="Souda",
           SIROS="Syros",LEVKAS="Lefkada",KATAKOLON="Katakolo",RHODOS="Rhodes",PATRAI="Patras",
           KAVALLA="Kavala",IRAKLION="Heraklion",KALAMAI="Kalamata",THESSALONIKI="Thessaloniki",
           PREVEZA="Preveza",ALEXANDROUPOLIS="Alexandroupoli",LEROS="Leros",
           `KHALKIS NORTH`="Chalkida North",`KHALKIS SOUTH`="Chalkida South",
           `CORFU ( KERKYRA )`="Corfu",`NORTH SALAMINOS`="Salamina",RAFINA="Rafina",
           SKOPELOS="Skopelos",`SAMOS ISLAND - VATHI`="Samos",`SOUDHAS II`="Souda II",
           `IRAKLION II`="Heraklion II",`RHODOS II`="Rhodes II",`NORTH SALAMINOS II`="Salamina II")
gauges<-stations[long_enough,]
gauges$rate<-gauge_rates
gauges$years<-recent_years[long_enough]
gauges$label<-ifelse(gauges$name%in%names(english),english[gauges$name],gauges$name)
gauges$hover<-paste0(gauges$label,": ",ifelse(gauges$rate>0,"+",""),mm_year(gauges$rate),
                     " since ",from," (",gauges$years," years)")
# the names of harbours close to each other go on opposite sides of their dots
sides<-c(`KHALKIS NORTH`="top center",`KHALKIS SOUTH`="bottom center",PREVEZA="top center",
         LEVKAS="bottom center",POSIDHONIA="middle left",PIRAIEVS="middle right")
gauges$side<-ifelse(gauges$name%in%names(sides),sides[gauges$name],"top center")
limit<-max(abs(gauges$rate))
plot_ly(gauges,type="scattergeo",mode="markers+text",lon=~lon,lat=~lat,text=~label,
        textposition=~side,textfont=list(size=11,color=dark_gray),
        marker=list(size=13,color=~rate,colorscale=list(c(0,blue),c(0.5,"#f2f2f2"),c(1,greek_red)),
                    cmin=-limit,cmax=limit,line=list(color=dark_gray,width=0.5),
                    colorbar=list(title=list(text="mm a year"),thickness=12)),
        hovertext=~hover,hovertemplate="%{hovertext}<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Sea level against the land since ",from,", mm a year"),
        paste0("PSMSL: the tide gauges of Greece with at least 15 yearly means since ",from,
               "; a straight line through each"),
        geo=list(resolution=50,showland=TRUE,landcolor="#f7f7f7",showocean=TRUE,
                 oceancolor="#eef4fa",showcountries=TRUE,countrycolor="#c8c8c8",
                 coastlinecolor="#b0b0b0",lonaxis=list(range=c(19,29)),
                 lataxis=list(range=c(34.5,41.8)),projection=list(type="mercator")),
        margin=list(t=60,b=60,l=10,r=10),note_y=-0.03)

Interactive chart: Sea level against the land since 2000, mm a year

Code 
gauges<-gauges[order(-gauges$rate),]
knitr::kable(data.frame(harbour=gauges$label,rate=paste0(ifelse(gauges$rate>0,"+",""),
                                                         mm_year(gauges$rate)),
                        years=gauges$years),
             col.names=c("Harbour",paste("Sea against the land since",from),"Yearly means"),
             align="lrr",row.names=FALSE)
Harbour Sea against the land since 2000 Yearly means
Corfu +4.9 mm a year 17
Leros +4.9 mm a year 23
Thessaloniki +4.2 mm a year 16
Preveza +3.9 mm a year 20
Piraeus +3.3 mm a year 26
Chalkida South +3.2 mm a year 15
Lefkada +3.2 mm a year 21
Souda +2.6 mm a year 19
Alexandroupoli +2.3 mm a year 22
Syros +2.0 mm a year 20
Posidonia +2.0 mm a year 19
Chalkida North +1.9 mm a year 21
Katakolo +0.2 mm a year 18

At all 13 harbours the sea rose against the land; the median rise was 3.2 mm a year, about the same as the 2.9 mm a year of the Mediterranean as a whole. The differences come mostly from the land. At Katakolo, at the bottom of the table, the sea rose least; at Corfu, at the top, the sea rose fastest, perhaps because the land there sinks. Greece lies where the African plate dives under the Aegean, and it is one of the most active corners of Europe for earthquakes (see Where the Earth Shakes).

5. Is the rise speeding up?

Yes. The satellites have now watched the oceans for more than thirty years, long enough to see the rise grow faster. Straight lines through the first and the last ten years of their record:

Code 
first_ten<-1993:2002
last_ten<-(last_satellite-9):last_satellite
speeds<-data.frame(sea=c("World","Mediterranean"),
                   first=c(rise(world,min(first_ten),max(first_ten)),
                           rise(mediterranean,min(first_ten),max(first_ten))),
                   last=c(rise(world,min(last_ten),last_satellite),
                          rise(mediterranean,min(last_ten),last_satellite)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(sea=speeds$sea,first=mm_year(speeds$first),last=mm_year(speeds$last)),
             col.names=c("Sea","1993–2002",paste0(min(last_ten),"–",last_satellite)),align="lrr")
Sea 1993–2002 2015–2024
World 2.8 mm a year 3.9 mm a year
Mediterranean 3.3 mm a year 6.5 mm a year
Code 
# the acceleration of the world's rise: a parabola through all the passes, mm a year, every year
acceleration<-2*unname(coef(lm(mm~time+I(time^2),world_passes))[3])

The world’s seas now rise by about 3.9 mm a year, against 2.8 mm a year in the 1990s. A parabola through all the passes of the satellites gives an acceleration of about 0.09 mm a year, every year. The Mediterranean moves more from decade to decade than the whole ocean, so its last ten years say less about the long run; but they too show a sea that rises faster than before.

6. How much higher could the sea be by 2100?

That depends mostly on how much more greenhouse gas the world emits. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) expects the world’s seas to stand, by 2100, 28 to 55 cm higher than in 1995–2014 if emissions fall to zero soon after 2050, and 63 to 101 cm higher if they keep rising fast. With very high emissions it cannot rule out a rise approaching two metres, because nobody knows yet how fast the ice sheets of Antarctica and Greenland could break up (IPCC 2021, B.5.3). The seas will keep rising for centuries after that, whatever happens to emissions, as the deep ocean warms slowly.

For Greece, with its coasts, ports, beaches and low deltas, even half a metre more means storms reaching further inland, and beaches that shrink; and where the land sinks, the sea rises faster still.

Sources

  • PSMSL: Tide gauge data, monthly means of the revised local reference (RLR) of every station; station 374, Piraeus, with its documentation. Holgate, S.J. and others (2013), New data systems and products at the Permanent Service for Mean Sea Level, Journal of Coastal Research 29, 493–504.
  • NOAA Laboratory for Satellite Altimetry: Sea level rise, time series of the global and regional mean sea level. Altimetry data are provided by NOAA Laboratory for Satellite Altimetry.
  • IPCC (2021), Summary for Policymakers, in Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis, Contribution of Working Group I to the Sixth Assessment Report: B.5.3 and its footnotes.

item.title: Why Did Olive Oil Get So Expensive? Prices, Harvests and the Drought in Spain
item.description: The price of extra virgin olive oil at the markets of Greece, Spain and Italy every week since 2010, the harvests of the four big producers of the EU, and what shoppers paid: why the price tripled in 2023 and 2024, and where it stands now.
item.content:encoded:
The price of extra virgin olive oil at the markets of Greece, Spain and Italy every week since 2010, the harvests of the four big producers of the EU, and what shoppers paid: why the price tripled in 2023 and 2024, and where it stands now.

What is this?

At the start of 2024 a kilo of extra virgin olive oil cost three times as much at the markets of Greece as it had a few years before. Greek families, who use more olive oil than almost anyone, felt it in the shops. This story follows the price and its causes with official data, in five questions:

  1. How much did olive oil cost?
  2. Why did the price triple?
  3. Why did Greek prices rise, when Greece had a good harvest?
  4. Did shoppers pay more?
  5. Where is the price now?

The prices and the harvests come from the agri-food data portal of the European Commission, which collects every week the prices that producers get at the main markets of each country. What shoppers paid comes from Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU. All are downloaded when the page is rendered.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("eurostat","jsonlite","plotly"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# the lines of a file on the web, tried again a few times: the servers sometimes refuse a connection
# or take too long to answer
read_lines<-function(url,tries=4) {
  for(k in seq_len(tries)) {
    result<-tryCatch(readLines(url,warn=FALSE),error=function(e) NULL)
    if(!is.null(result))
      return(result)
    Sys.sleep(10)
  }
  stop("Could not download ",url)
}
portal<-"https://ec.europa.eu/agrifood/api/oliveOil/"
# the price of extra virgin olive oil every week since 2010, the average of the markets of Greece,
# Spain and Italy, euros a kilo (the portal gives euros for 100 kg)
weekly<-jsonlite::fromJSON(paste(read_lines(paste0(portal,"prices?memberStateCodes=EL,ES,IT",
                                                   "&beginDate=01/01/2010",
                                                   "&products=Extra%20virgin%20olive%20oil",
                                                   "%20(up%20to%200.8%25)",
                                                   "&markets=Average%20national%20price")),
                                 collapse=""))
weekly<-data.frame(country=weekly$memberStateCode,
                   date=as.Date(weekly$beginDate,format="%d/%m/%Y"),
                   price=as.numeric(gsub("[€,]","",weekly$price))/100)
weekly<-weekly[order(weekly$country,weekly$date),]
greece<-weekly[weekly$country=="EL",]
spain<-weekly[weekly$country=="ES",]
# the normal years before the crisis, and the dearest week
normal<-greece$price[format(greece$date,"%Y")>="2015"&format(greece$date,"%Y")<="2021"]
base<-mean(normal)
peak_of<-function(country) {
  x<-weekly[weekly$country==country,]
  result<-x[which.max(x$price),]
  return(result)
}
peak<-peak_of("EL")
latest<-greece[nrow(greece),]
# how closely the Greek and Spanish prices of the same weeks move together
same_weeks<-merge(greece,spain,by="date",suffixes=c("_greece","_spain"))
together<-cor(same_weeks$price_greece,same_weeks$price_spain)
# the harvests of the four big producers of the EU, thousand tonnes of olive oil, by marketing year
# (October to September); the last years are estimates
harvests<-jsonlite::fromJSON(paste(read_lines(paste0(portal,"production",
                                                     "?memberStateCodes=EL,ES,IT,PT",
                                                     "&granularity=annual")),
                                   collapse=""))
harvests<-data.frame(country=harvests$memberStateCode,season=harvests$marketingYear,
                     tonnes=harvests$yearProductionQuantity,
                     estimate=harvests$isEstimated=="Y")
harvests<-harvests[order(harvests$country,harvests$season),]
crop<-function(country,season) {
  result<-harvests$tonnes[harvests$country==country&harvests$season==season]
  return(result)
}
# Spain's share of the four in the seasons before the drought that all four reported
seasons<-names(which(table(harvests$season[!harvests$estimate])==4))
before_drought<-seasons[seasons<"2022/23"]
four<-harvests[harvests$season%in%before_drought,]
spain_share<-100*sum(four$tonnes[four$country=="ES"])/sum(four$tonnes)
# what shoppers paid: Eurostat's index of the consumer prices of olive oil and of all food,
# 2015 = 100, every month. It stops in December 2025, when Eurostat moved to a new classification
# in which olive oil is no longer a group of its own
shops<-get_eurostat("prc_hicp_midx",filters=list(geo=c("EL","EU27_2020"),unit="I15",
                                                 coicop=c("CP01153","CP011")),
                    time_format="raw",cache=FALSE)
shops<-as.data.frame(shops[!is.na(shops$values),])
shops$date<-as.Date(paste0(shops$time,"-01"))
shops<-shops[order(shops$date),]
index<-function(geo,coicop,month) {
  result<-shops$values[shops$geo==geo&shops$coicop==coicop&format(shops$date,"%Y-%m")==month]
  return(result)
}
greek_oil<-shops[shops$geo=="EL"&shops$coicop=="CP01153",]
Code 
greek_red<-"#d62728"
blue<-"#1f77b4"
gray<-"#9e9e9e"
dark_gray<-"#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes and the labels
# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(),
                margin=list(t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.16,...) {
  note<-list(text=paste("Source:",source),xref="paper",yref="paper",x=0,y=note_y,xanchor="left",
             yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=11,color=dark_gray))
  result<-layout(p,
                 title=list(text=title,x=0.02,xanchor="left",y=0.97,yanchor="top"),
                 yaxis=c(list(title=y_title),y_axis),
                 xaxis=c(list(title=""),x_axis),
                 margin=margin,
                 annotations=c(annotations,list(note)),
                 ...) %>%
    config(displaylogo=FALSE)
  return(result)
}
legend_top<-list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.02,yanchor="bottom")
# the countries of the charts: Greece and Spain in colour, the others in gray
countries<-data.frame(code=c("EL","ES","IT","PT"),name=c("Greece","Spain","Italy","Portugal"),
                      color=c(greek_red,blue,gray,gray),dash=c("solid","solid","solid","dot"))
# short labels of numbers
euro<-function(x) {
  result<-paste0("€",format(round(x,2),nsmall=2,trim=TRUE))
  return(result)
}
thousand<-function(x) {
  result<-paste0(format(round(x)*1000,big.mark=",",trim=TRUE)," tonnes")
  return(result)
}
day<-function(date) {
  result<-trimws(format(date,"%e %B %Y"))
  return(result)
}

1. How much did olive oil cost?

About €2.98 a kilo in 2015–2021, and €8.91 at the peak. These are the prices that producers got for extra virgin olive oil at the main markets of each country, in bulk, before bottling, transport and the shop’s margin. In the week of 8 January 2024 the average of the Greek markets reached €8.91 a kilo, 3.0 times the average of 2015–2021. Spain and Italy peaked in the same month, at €9.03 and €9.61.

Code 
p<-plot_ly()
for(k in 1:3) {
  x<-weekly[weekly$country==countries$code[k],]
  p<-p %>%
    add_trace(data=x,x=~date,y=~price,type="scatter",mode="lines",name=countries$name[k],
              line=list(color=countries$color[k],width=if(k<3) 2 else 1.5),
              hovertemplate=paste0(countries$name[k],": €%{y:.2f}<extra></extra>"))
}
p %>%
  chart("Extra virgin olive oil at the markets, euros a kilo",
        paste0("EU agri-food data portal: the average of each country's markets, every week, ",
               "January 2010 to ",format(max(weekly$date),"%B %Y")),
        "Euros a kilo",hovermode="x unified",legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90),
        y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero"))

Interactive chart: Extra virgin olive oil at the markets, euros a kilo

The average price of each year at the Greek markets:

Code 
years<-aggregate(price~year,transform(greece,year=format(date,"%Y")),mean)
years<-years[years$year>="2015",]
knitr::kable(data.frame(year=years$year,price=euro(years$price),
                        times=format(round(years$price/base,1),nsmall=1)),
             col.names=c("Year","Euros a kilo","Times the average of 2015–2021"),align="lrr")
Year Euros a kilo Times the average of 2015–2021
2015 €3.23 1.1
2016 €3.12 1.0
2017 €3.72 1.2
2018 €2.94 1.0
2019 €2.60 0.9
2020 €2.26 0.8
2021 €3.05 1.0
2022 €3.62 1.2
2023 €6.40 2.1
2024 €7.30 2.4
2025 €4.20 1.4
2026 €3.97 1.3

2. Why did the price triple?

Because Spain, which makes most of Europe’s olive oil, lost more than half of its harvest to drought. In the seasons from 2013/14 to 2021/22, Spain made 67% of the olive oil of the four big producers of the EU. After a year of drought and record heat, its harvest fell from 1,491,000 tonnes in 2021/22 to 666,000 tonnes in 2022/23, 55% less, and stayed low in 2023/24 with 855,000 tonnes. Buyers bid up the price of what there was.

Code 
p<-plot_ly()
for(k in 1:4) {
  x<-harvests[harvests$country==countries$code[k],]
  p<-p %>%
    add_trace(data=x,x=~season,y=~tonnes,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers",
              name=countries$name[k],
              line=list(color=countries$color[k],width=2,dash=countries$dash[k]),
              marker=list(color=countries$color[k],size=7,
                          symbol=ifelse(x$estimate,"circle-open","circle")),
              hovertemplate=paste0(countries$name[k],": %{y:,.0f} thousand tonnes<extra></extra>"))
}
p %>%
  chart("Olive oil harvests, thousand tonnes",
        paste("European Commission, agri-food data portal. Seasons from October to September;",
              "open circles: estimates."),
        "Thousand tonnes",hovermode="x unified",legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90),
        x_axis=list(type="category"))

Interactive chart: Olive oil harvests, thousand tonnes

3. Why did Greek prices rise, when Greece had a good harvest?

Because olive oil is sold in one European market. Greece made 346,000 tonnes in 2022/23, more than in an average season; yet the Greek price rose with the Spanish one. Traders buy where the oil is cheapest, and much Greek oil is sold in bulk to Italian bottlers. So the prices of the three countries move together: the weekly prices of Greece and Spain since 2010 have a correlation of 0.99 (1 would mean that they always move together). Then, in 2023/24, the Greek harvest fell too, to 192,000 tonnes.

4. Did shoppers pay more?

Yes, a lot more, though less than the markets. Eurostat’s index of the price of olive oil in Greek shops rose by 139% from January 2021 to its peak in July 2024. The price at the markets is only part of what a shopper pays: bottling, transport, taxes and the margins of the shops are the rest, and they did not triple. All food in Greece rose by 35% from January 2021 to December 2025.

Code 
lines<-data.frame(geo=c("EL","EU27_2020","EL"),coicop=c("CP01153","CP01153","CP011"),
                  name=c("Olive oil, Greece","Olive oil, EU-27","All food, Greece"),
                  color=c(greek_red,blue,dark_gray),dash=c("solid","solid","dot"))
p<-plot_ly()
for(k in seq_len(nrow(lines))) {
  # from 2015, the first year of the index of olive oil
  x<-shops[shops$geo==lines$geo[k]&shops$coicop==lines$coicop[k]&shops$date>=as.Date("2015-01-01"),]
  p<-p %>%
    add_trace(data=x,x=~date,y=~values,type="scatter",mode="lines",name=lines$name[k],
              line=list(color=lines$color[k],width=2,dash=lines$dash[k]),
              hovertemplate=paste0(lines$name[k],": %{y:.1f}<extra></extra>"))
}
p %>%
  chart("Consumer prices, 2015 = 100",
        paste0("Eurostat, prc_hicp_midx (harmonised index of consumer prices), every month to ",
               format(max(shops$date),"%B %Y")),
        "Index, 2015 = 100",hovermode="x unified",legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90))

Interactive chart: Consumer prices, 2015 = 100

5. Where is the price now?

Back near where it was before the drought. Spain’s harvest recovered in 2024/25, to 1,421,000 tonnes, and the price fell with it. In the week of 9 November 2026 a kilo of extra virgin olive oil fetched €3.26 at the Greek markets, 1.1 times the average of 2015–2021 and 63% below the peak. In the shops, prices fall more slowly: in December 2025 the Greek index of olive oil was still 45% above January 2021.

The lesson of these years is that the price of olive oil depends less on any one country than on the weather of Spain, and as droughts and heatwaves become more common around the Mediterranean (see Athens Is Getting Hotter), years like 2023 may come again.

Sources

  • European Commission, agri-food data portal: olive oil prices and olive oil production, through its API.
  • Eurostat: prc_hicp_midx (harmonised index of consumer prices, monthly).

item.title: Are Greek Roads Getting Safer? Road Deaths in Greece Since 1999
item.description: Road deaths in Greece in Eurostat data since 1999: how far they fell, how Greece compares with the EU, why motorcyclists and young men die most, which regions are the most dangerous, and whether Greece can still halve its road deaths by 2030.
item.content:encoded:
Road deaths in Greece in Eurostat data since 1999: how far they fell, how Greece compares with the EU, why motorcyclists and young men die most, which regions are the most dangerous, and whether Greece can still halve its road deaths by 2030.

What is this?

Greek roads used to be among the most dangerous in Europe. This story asks how much safer they have become, with official data, in six questions:

  1. How many people die on Greek roads?
  2. How does Greece compare with the EU?
  3. Who dies?
  4. Why young men?
  5. Where are the roads most dangerous?
  6. Will Greece halve its road deaths by 2030?

The data come from Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU, which collects the road deaths that the police of each country record: a road death is a person killed on the spot or within 30 days of a road accident. They are downloaded when the page is rendered, so a new render brings in the latest year.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("eurostat","plotly"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values; the year as a number
eurostat_values<-function(id,filters) {
  x<-get_eurostat(id,filters=filters,time_format="num",cache=FALSE)
  result<-as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values),])
  return(result)
}
# people killed on the roads by age and sex, in number and per million inhabitants, for every
# country of the EU
killed<-eurostat_values("tran_sf_roadus",list(pers_cat="TOTAL",unit=c("NR","P_MHAB")))
total<-killed[killed$sex=="T"&killed$age=="TOTAL",]
deaths<-function(geo,year,unit="NR") {
  result<-total$values[total$geo==geo&total$time==year&total$unit==unit]
  return(result)
}
greece<-total[total$geo=="EL"&total$unit=="NR",]
greece<-greece[order(greece$time),]
first<-min(greece$time)
last<-max(greece$time)
eu_name<-c(setNames(eu_countries$name,eu_countries$code),EU27_2020="EU-27")
rates<-total[total$unit=="P_MHAB"&total$time==last&total$geo%in%names(eu_name),]
rates$name<-eu_name[rates$geo]
countries<-rates[rates$geo!="EU27_2020",]
countries<-countries[order(-countries$values),]
rank<-match("EL",countries$geo)
# the deaths per million people of an age group in the last year
age_rate<-function(geo,age) {
  result<-killed$values[killed$geo==geo&killed$sex=="T"&killed$age==age&
                          killed$unit=="P_MHAB"&killed$time==last]
  return(result)
}
# people killed by the vehicle they were in or on; the groups of the codes do not overlap, so they
# add up to the total. Those killed outside a vehicle, mostly pedestrians, are "OTH"
vehicles<-eurostat_values("tran_sf_roadve",list(geo=c("EL","EU27_2020"),unit="NR"))
groups<-list(`Car occupants`="CAR",
             `Motorcyclists and moped riders`=c("MOTO_2WH","MOTO_LE125","MOTO_GT125","MOTO_NSP",
                                                "MOP"),
             Cyclists=c("BIKE","EPAC"),
             `Lorries and vans`=c("VG_LE3P5","VG_GT3P5","VEH_GD"),
             `Pedestrians and others`=NA)
# the deaths of each group, by country and year: the last group takes what the others leave
by_group<-do.call(rbind,lapply(c("EL","EU27_2020"),function(geo) {
  x<-vehicles[vehicles$geo==geo,]
  do.call(rbind,lapply(sort(unique(x$time)),function(year) {
    y<-x[x$time==year,]
    all<-sum(y$values[y$vehicle=="TOTAL"])
    counts<-sapply(groups[-length(groups)],function(codes) sum(y$values[y$vehicle%in%codes]))
    data.frame(geo=geo,time=year,group=names(groups),
               deaths=c(counts,all-sum(counts)),total=all)
  }))
}))
recent<-by_group[by_group$time>last-5,]
share<-function(geo,group) {
  x<-recent[recent$geo==geo,]
  result<-100*sum(x$deaths[x$group==group])/sum(x$deaths)
  return(result)
}
motorcycles<-by_group[by_group$geo=="EL"&by_group$group=="Motorcyclists and moped riders",]
cars<-by_group[by_group$geo=="EL"&by_group$group=="Car occupants",]
riders_rose<-tail(motorcycles$deaths,1)>motorcycles$deaths[motorcycles$time==2019]
# the deaths of each region of Greece per million inhabitants, the average of the last years
regions<-eurostat_values("tran_r_acci",list(victim="KIL",unit="P_MHAB"))
regions<-regions[substr(regions$geo,1,2)=="EL"&nchar(regions$geo)==4,]
region_last<-max(regions$time)
regions<-regions[regions$time>region_last-4,]
# the rate of Greece as a whole over the same years
greece_rate<-mean(total$values[total$geo=="EL"&total$unit=="P_MHAB"&
                                 total$time%in%unique(regions$time)])
Code 
greek_red<-"#d62728"
blue<-"#1f77b4"
gray<-"#9e9e9e"
dark_gray<-"#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes and the labels
# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(),
                margin=list(t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.16,...) {
  note<-list(text=paste("Source:",source),xref="paper",yref="paper",x=0,y=note_y,xanchor="left",
             yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=11,color=dark_gray))
  result<-layout(p,
                 title=list(text=title,x=0.02,xanchor="left",y=0.97,yanchor="top"),
                 yaxis=c(list(title=y_title),y_axis),
                 xaxis=c(list(title=""),x_axis),
                 margin=margin,
                 annotations=c(annotations,list(note)),
                 ...) %>%
    config(displaylogo=FALSE)
  return(result)
}
legend_top<-list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.02,yanchor="bottom")
# short labels of numbers
number<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x),big.mark=",",trim=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
ordinal<-function(n) {
  suffix<-ifelse(n%%100%in%11:13,"th",c("th","st","nd","rd",rep("th",6))[n%%10+1])
  result<-paste0(n,suffix)
  return(result)
}

1. How many people die on Greek roads?

69% fewer than in 1999. In 1999, 2,116 people died on the roads of Greece; in 2024, 664. Most of the fall came before 2015: part of it with the economic crisis, which took cars off the roads, and part with safer cars, better roads and more checks by the police. Since then the fall has slowed: 793 people died in 2015, 584 in 2020, when the pandemic emptied the roads, and 664 in 2024.

Code 
plot_ly(greece,x=~time,y=~values,type="bar",marker=list(color=greek_red),
        hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:,.0f} killed<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("People killed on Greek roads each year",
        paste0("Eurostat, tran_sf_roadus, ",first,"–",last,
               ": killed on the spot or within 30 days"),
        "People killed")

Interactive chart: People killed on Greek roads each year

2. How does Greece compare with the EU?

Better than before, but still among the worst. Counted per million inhabitants, 197 people died on Greek roads in 1999, against 128 in the EU as a whole. In 2024 the figures were 64 and 44: Greece had the 3rd highest rate of the 27 countries, after Romania and Bulgaria.

Code 
rates<-rates[order(rates$values),]
plot_ly(rates,x=~values,y=~factor(name,levels=name),type="bar",orientation="h",
        marker=list(color=ifelse(rates$geo=="EL",greek_red,
                                 ifelse(rates$geo=="EU27_2020",blue,gray))),
        text=~round(values),textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE,
        hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x:.0f} killed per million inhabitants<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Road deaths per million inhabitants, ",last),"Eurostat, tran_sf_roadus",
        margin=list(l=130,t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.08)

Interactive chart: Road deaths per million inhabitants, 2024

Code 
trend<-total[total$unit=="P_MHAB"&total$geo%in%c("EL","EU27_2020"),]
trend<-trend[order(trend$time),]
plot_ly(trend[trend$geo=="EL",],x=~time,y=~values,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers",
        name="Greece",line=list(color=greek_red,width=2),marker=list(color=greek_red,size=7),
        hovertemplate="Greece: %{y:.0f}<extra></extra>") %>%
  add_trace(data=trend[trend$geo=="EU27_2020",],name="EU-27",line=list(color=blue,width=2),
            marker=list(color=blue,size=7),hovertemplate="EU-27: %{y:.0f}<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("Road deaths per million inhabitants","Eurostat, tran_sf_roadus","Killed per million",
        hovermode="x unified",legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90),
        y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero"))

Interactive chart: Road deaths per million inhabitants

3. Who dies?

More and more, motorcyclists. In 2020–2024, 38% of the people killed on Greek roads were riding a motorcycle or a moped, against 20% in the EU. Motorcycles are everywhere in Greece, for its mild weather, its narrow streets and its delivery riders; and a rider has no body of metal around them.

Code 
shares<-aggregate(deaths~geo+group,recent,sum)
shares$percent<-100*shares$deaths/ave(shares$deaths,shares$geo,FUN=sum)
shares$group<-factor(shares$group,levels=rev(names(groups)))
plot_ly(shares[shares$geo=="EL",],x=~percent,y=~group,type="bar",orientation="h",name="Greece",
        marker=list(color=greek_red),text=~paste0(round(percent),"%"),textposition="outside",
        cliponaxis=FALSE,hovertemplate="Greece, %{y}: %{x:.1f}%<extra></extra>") %>%
  add_trace(data=shares[shares$geo=="EU27_2020",],name="EU-27",marker=list(color=blue),
            hovertemplate="EU-27, %{y}: %{x:.1f}%<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Who was killed on the roads, ",last-4,"–",last,", % of the deaths"),
        "Eurostat, tran_sf_roadve: the vehicle that each person killed was in or on",
        barmode="group",legend=legend_top,margin=list(l=210,t=100,b=90),
        x_axis=list(range=c(0,1.2*max(shares$percent))))

Interactive chart: Who was killed on the roads, 2020–2024, % of the deaths

The motorcyclists are also why the fall slowed. Since 1999, the deaths of people in cars fell by 73%, those of motorcyclists and moped riders by only 49%; and since 2019 the riders killed went from 247 to 287. In 1999 they were 27% of all road deaths in Greece, in 2024 43%.

Code 
plot_ly(cars,x=~time,y=~deaths,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers",name="Car occupants",
        line=list(color=dark_gray,width=2),marker=list(color=dark_gray,size=7),
        hovertemplate="Car occupants: %{y:,.0f}<extra></extra>") %>%
  add_trace(data=motorcycles,name="Motorcyclists and moped riders",
            line=list(color=greek_red,width=2),marker=list(color=greek_red,size=7),
            hovertemplate="Motorcyclists and moped riders: %{y:,.0f}<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("People killed in cars and on two wheels in Greece","Eurostat, tran_sf_roadve",
        "People killed",hovermode="x unified",legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90),
        y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero"))

Interactive chart: People killed in cars and on two wheels in Greece

4. Why young men?

Everywhere, the young and men are the most at risk on the roads: the young lack experience, and both take more risks; men also drive more. 84% of the people killed on Greek roads in 2020–2024 were men. And counted per million people of each age, the young die most: in 2024, 122 people aged 18 to 24 died per million of their age in Greece, against 72 in the EU.

Code 
ages<-c(Y_LT15="Under 15",`Y15-17`="15–17",`Y18-24`="18–24",`Y25-49`="25–49",
        `Y50-64`="50–64",Y_GE65="65 and over")
by_age<-killed[killed$sex=="T"&killed$unit=="P_MHAB"&killed$time==last&
                 killed$geo%in%c("EL","EU27_2020")&killed$age%in%names(ages),]
by_age$label<-factor(ages[by_age$age],levels=ages)
plot_ly(by_age[by_age$geo=="EL",],x=~label,y=~values,type="bar",name="Greece",
        marker=list(color=greek_red),hovertemplate="Greece, %{x}: %{y:.0f}<extra></extra>") %>%
  add_trace(data=by_age[by_age$geo=="EU27_2020",],name="EU-27",marker=list(color=blue),
            hovertemplate="EU-27, %{x}: %{y:.0f}<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Road deaths per million people of each age, ",last),"Eurostat, tran_sf_roadus",
        "Killed per million",barmode="group",legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90))

Interactive chart: Road deaths per million people of each age, 2024

5. Where are the roads most dangerous?

On the islands and in the regions of long country roads; least in Attica. Per million inhabitants, the average of 2020–2023:

Code 
english<-c(EL30="Attica",EL41="North Aegean",EL42="South Aegean",EL43="Crete",
           EL51="Eastern Macedonia and Thrace",EL52="Central Macedonia",EL53="Western Macedonia",
           EL54="Epirus",EL61="Thessaly",EL62="Ionian Islands",EL63="Western Greece",
           EL64="Central Greece",EL65="Peloponnese")
average<-aggregate(values~geo,regions,mean)
average$name<-ifelse(average$geo%in%names(english),english[average$geo],average$geo)
average<-average[order(average$values),]
plot_ly(average,x=~values,y=~factor(name,levels=name),type="bar",orientation="h",
        marker=list(color=ifelse(average$values>greece_rate,greek_red,gray)),
        text=~round(values),textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE,
        hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x:.0f} killed per million inhabitants<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Road deaths per million inhabitants, ",region_last-3,"–",region_last),
        "Eurostat, tran_r_acci. In red: above the rate of Greece as a whole.",
        margin=list(l=230,t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.1)

Interactive chart: Road deaths per million inhabitants, 2020–2023

Attica, with its city streets and slower traffic, has the lowest rate: 45 per million. The highest is that of the South Aegean, 113. The islands count the deaths of their summer visitors, who drive and ride rented vehicles on roads they do not know, against their residents only, so their rates come out higher than the risk of their own people.

6. Will Greece halve its road deaths by 2030?

The EU has set itself the goal of halving the road deaths of 2019 by 2030, on the way to Vision Zero, close to no road deaths by 2050 (European Commission 2020). For Greece that means no more than 344 deaths in 2030, from 688 in 2019.

Code 
path<-data.frame(time=2019:2030,values=deaths("EL",2019)*(1-0.5*(0:11)/11))
recent_years<-greece[greece$time>=2010,]
plot_ly(recent_years,x=~time,y=~values,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers",name="Deaths",
        line=list(color=greek_red,width=2),marker=list(color=greek_red,size=7),
        hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:,.0f} killed<extra></extra>") %>%
  add_trace(data=path,name="Path to half by 2030",line=list(color=dark_gray,width=2,dash="dash"),
            marker=list(color=dark_gray,size=5),
            hovertemplate="%{x}, on the path: %{y:,.0f}<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("Greek road deaths and the goal of 2030","Eurostat, tran_sf_roadus; the EU's goal for 2030",
        "People killed",legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90),y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero"))

Interactive chart: Greek road deaths and the goal of 2030

On present trends, no. By 2024 Greece should have been down to 532 deaths to stay on the straight path; it had 664, 3% fewer than in 2019 instead of 23%. To reach the goal, the deaths would have to fall by 10% a year from now on. The fastest way there runs through the motorcyclists: they were 43% of the dead in 2024, and theirs are the deaths that rose since 2019.

Sources

  • Eurostat: tran_sf_roadus (persons killed in road accidents by type of road user, age and sex), tran_sf_roadve (persons killed by type of vehicle), tran_r_acci (victims of road accidents by NUTS 2 region).
  • European Commission (2020), EU Road Safety Policy Framework 2021–2030: Next steps towards “Vision Zero”, SWD(2019) 283; see the Commission’s road safety pages.

item.content:encoded:
Weekly deaths in Greece in Eurostat data, against the deaths a normal year would bring: the pandemic, the heatwaves, who died, how Greece compares with the EU, and why fewer people have died since 2024.

What is this?

Counting the deaths of a disease is hard: doctors must decide what each person died of, and countries decide it in different ways. Counting all deaths is easy, and every EU country reports them to Eurostat week by week. The deaths above what a normal week would bring are the excess deaths: they include the deaths of the disease that nobody recorded as such, and the deaths that a heatwave or an overwhelmed hospital caused.

This story compares the deaths of every week in Greece since 2015 with the deaths a normal year would have brought, and answers seven questions:

  1. How many people die in Greece in a normal week?
  2. How many more died during the pandemic?
  3. Which weeks were the worst?
  4. Does the heat kill too?
  5. Who died?
  6. How does Greece compare with the EU?
  7. What came after the pandemic?

The deaths come from Eurostat, the temperatures of Athens from ERA5-Land, a reconstruction of the weather of every day by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. Both are downloaded when the page is rendered, so a new render brings in the latest weeks.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("eurostat","plotly"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values; the time as text: "2024-W05", "2024-05"
eurostat_values<-function(id,filters) {
  x<-get_eurostat(id,filters=filters,time_format="raw",cache=FALSE)
  result<-as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values),])
  result$time<-as.character(result$time)
  return(result)
}
# the Monday that an ISO week ("2024-W05") starts on: week 1 is the week with 4 January in it
week_monday<-function(time) {
  january_4<-as.Date(paste0(substr(time,1,4),"-01-04"))
  result<-january_4-(as.integer(format(january_4,"%u"))-1)+7*(as.integer(substr(time,7,8))-1)
  return(result)
}
# deaths in Greece every week since 2015, all ages
weekly<-eurostat_values("demo_r_mwk_ts",list(geo="EL",sex="T"))
weekly<-weekly[order(weekly$time),c("time","values")]
names(weekly)[2]<-"deaths"
weekly$year<-as.integer(substr(weekly$time,1,4))
weekly$week<-as.integer(substr(weekly$time,7,8))
weekly$monday<-week_monday(weekly$time)
# deaths every week by age, in ten-year groups
by_age<-eurostat_values("demo_r_mwk_10",list(geo="EL",sex="T"))
# Eurostat's own measure: the deaths of each month against the average of the same month in
# 2016-2019, %, for every EU country
eurostat_excess<-eurostat_values("demo_mexrt",list(unit="PC"))
# the highest temperature of every day in Athens since 2015, from ERA5-Land through Open-Meteo, as
# one CSV file: two lines about the point of the grid, an empty line, then the days
weather_url<-paste0("https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive",
                    "?latitude=37.98&longitude=23.73&start_date=2015-01-01&end_date=",
                    Sys.Date()-1,"&daily=temperature_2m_max&timezone=Europe%2FAthens",
                    "&models=era5_land&format=csv")
weather<-read.csv(text=readLines(weather_url)[-(1:3)],col.names=c("date","tmax"))
weather<-weather[!is.na(weather$tmax),] # the last few days are not ready yet
weather$time<-format(as.Date(weather$date),"%G-W%V")
# the average of the highest temperatures of each week
heat<-aggregate(tmax~time,weather,mean)
weekly$tmax<-heat$tmax[match(weekly$time,heat$time)]

The deaths a normal year would bring

A normal week has more deaths in winter, when flu and the cold strike, than in summer, and the deaths of a normal year grow slowly as the population gets older. So the expected deaths of each week come from a model of the five years before the pandemic, 2015–2019: each week of the year has its own level, and every year adds the same share to all of them. It is a Poisson regression, the usual model for counts, with a dispersion that is allowed to be larger than Poisson’s. The years 53 weeks long count their last week as week 52.

Code 
# the expected deaths of every week, from the weeks of 2015-2019, and how far a normal week may
# stray from them: twice the standard deviation of the model
expect<-function(x) {
  x$season<-factor(pmin(x$week,52))
  before<-x[x$year<=2019,]
  model<-glm(deaths~year+season,family=quasipoisson,data=before)
  x$expected<-predict(model,newdata=x,type="response")
  spread<-2*sqrt(summary(model)$dispersion*x$expected)
  x$low<-x$expected-spread
  x$high<-x$expected+spread
  x$excess<-x$deaths-x$expected
  x$percent<-100*x$excess/x$expected
  result<-list(weeks=x,growth=100*(exp(coef(model)[["year"]])-1))
  return(result)
}
fitted<-expect(weekly)
weekly<-fitted$weeks
# the deaths of every year: what was expected, what happened, and the difference
years<-data.frame(year=sort(unique(weekly$year)))
years$weeks<-as.vector(table(weekly$year)[as.character(years$year)])
years$deaths<-as.vector(tapply(weekly$deaths,weekly$year,sum))
years$expected<-as.vector(tapply(weekly$expected,weekly$year,sum))
years$excess<-years$deaths-years$expected
years$percent<-100*years$excess/years$expected
at<-function(column,year) {
  result<-years[[column]][years$year==year]
  return(result)
}
pandemic<-years[years$year%in%2020:2022,]
last_full<-max(years$year[years$weeks>=52])
# the weeks with the most and the fewest expected deaths in 2019
normal<-weekly[weekly$year==2019,]
peak<-normal[which.max(normal$expected),]
trough<-normal[which.min(normal$expected),]
# the deaths of the last full year against an average year of 2016-2019, % (all 52 weeks long),
# and Eurostat's measure for the same year
before_average<-mean(years$deaths[years$year%in%2016:2019])
after_change<-100*(at("deaths",last_full)/before_average-1)
eurostat_last<-mean(eurostat_excess$values[eurostat_excess$geo=="EL"&
                                             substr(eurostat_excess$time,1,4)==last_full])
Code 
greek_red<-"#d62728"
blue<-"#1f77b4"
gray<-"#9e9e9e"
dark_gray<-"#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes and the labels
# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(),
                margin=list(t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.16,...) {
  note<-list(text=paste("Source:",source),xref="paper",yref="paper",x=0,y=note_y,xanchor="left",
             yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=11,color=dark_gray))
  result<-layout(p,
                 title=list(text=title,x=0.02,xanchor="left",y=0.97,yanchor="top"),
                 yaxis=c(list(title=y_title),y_axis),
                 xaxis=c(list(title=""),x_axis),
                 margin=margin,
                 annotations=c(annotations,list(note)),
                 ...) %>%
    config(displaylogo=FALSE)
  return(result)
}
legend_top<-list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.02,yanchor="bottom")
# short labels of numbers
number<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x),big.mark=",",trim=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
percent<-function(x,digits=0,sign=FALSE) {
  result<-paste0(ifelse(sign&x>0,"+",""),format(round(x,digits),nsmall=digits,trim=TRUE),"%")
  return(result)
}
# a week in words: "15–21 July 2024"
week_dates<-function(monday) {
  sunday<-monday+6
  start<-ifelse(format(monday,"%m")==format(sunday,"%m"),format(monday,"%e"),
                format(monday,"%e %B"))
  result<-paste0(trimws(start),"–",trimws(format(sunday,"%e %B %Y")))
  return(result)
}
ordinal<-function(n) {
  suffix<-ifelse(n%%100%in%11:13,"th",c("th","st","nd","rd",rep("th",6))[n%%10+1])
  result<-paste0(n,suffix)
  return(result)
}

1. How many people die in Greece in a normal week?

About 2,340. In 2015–2019 Greece recorded 121,669 deaths in a year of 52 weeks. The worst weeks of a normal year come in winter, with flu and the cold: for a week of January the model expects about 3,020 deaths, for a week of September about 2,020. And as the population ages, the expected deaths grow by about 0.8% a year.

2. How many more died during the pandemic?

About 38,400 in 2020–2022, 10% more than a normal three years would have brought. The worst year was 2021, with 18,380 deaths more than expected (+15%). In the chart, the gray band is the range in which a normal week falls; the red line is what happened.

Code 
plot_ly(weekly,x=~monday) %>%
  add_trace(y=~high,type="scatter",mode="lines",line=list(width=0),hoverinfo="skip",
            showlegend=FALSE) %>%
  add_trace(y=~low,type="scatter",mode="lines",line=list(width=0),fill="tonexty",
            fillcolor="rgba(158,158,158,0.3)",name="Normal range",hoverinfo="skip") %>%
  add_trace(y=~expected,type="scatter",mode="lines",name="Expected",
            line=list(color=dark_gray,width=1,dash="dot"),
            hovertemplate="Expected: %{y:,.0f}<extra></extra>") %>%
  add_trace(y=~deaths,type="scatter",mode="lines",name="Deaths",
            line=list(color=greek_red,width=1.5),
            hovertemplate="Deaths: %{y:,.0f}<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("Deaths in Greece every week",
        paste0("Eurostat, demo_r_mwk_ts, January 2015 to the week of ",
               week_dates(weekly$monday[nrow(weekly)]),"; expected: the model above"),
        "Deaths a week",hovermode="x unified",
        legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90),note_y=-0.12)

Interactive chart: Deaths in Greece every week

The same by year. 2026 has 27 weeks so far. 2015 and 2020 had 53 weeks, and so more deaths and more expected deaths than the other years.

Code 
plot_ly(years,x=~year,y=~excess,type="bar",
        marker=list(color=ifelse(years$excess>0,greek_red,blue)),
        text=~percent(percent,sign=TRUE),textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE,
        hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:,.0f} deaths more than expected<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("Deaths above (+) or below (−) the expected, each year",
        "Eurostat, demo_r_mwk_ts; the expected deaths from the model above","Deaths",
        x_axis=list(dtick=1))

Interactive chart: Deaths above (+) or below (−) the expected, each year

Code 
knitr::kable(data.frame(year=years$year,weeks=years$weeks,deaths=number(years$deaths),
                        expected=number(years$expected),excess=number(years$excess),
                        percent=percent(years$percent,1,sign=TRUE)),
             col.names=c("Year","Weeks","Deaths","Expected","Excess","Excess, %"),align="r")
Year Weeks Deaths Expected Excess Excess, %
2015 53 123,324 122,175 1,149 +0.9%
2016 52 118,116 120,549 -2,433 -2.0%
2017 52 124,069 121,482 2,587 +2.1%
2018 52 119,952 122,423 -2,471 -2.0%
2019 52 124,538 123,370 1,168 +0.9%
2020 53 132,969 126,978 5,991 +4.7%
2021 52 143,668 125,288 18,380 +14.7%
2022 52 140,292 126,257 14,035 +11.1%
2023 52 127,671 127,235 436 +0.3%
2024 52 126,182 128,220 -2,038 -1.6%
2025 52 121,566 129,212 -7,646 -5.9%
2026 27 64,952 70,169 -5,217 -7.4%

3. Which weeks were the worst?

The ten weeks with the most deaths above the expected:

Code 
worst<-weekly[order(-weekly$excess),][1:10,]
hot_weeks<-worst$week>=23&worst$week<=39 # June to September
knitr::kable(data.frame(week=week_dates(worst$monday),deaths=number(worst$deaths),
                        expected=number(worst$expected),
                        excess=percent(worst$percent,sign=TRUE),
                        heat=paste0(format(round(worst$tmax,1),nsmall=1)," °C")),
             col.names=c("Week","Deaths","Expected","Excess","Athens, average highest temperature"),
             align="lrrrr")
Week Deaths Expected Excess Athens, average highest temperature
2–8 August 2021 3,895 2,419 +61% 38.6 °C
15–21 July 2024 3,268 2,266 +44% 36.8 °C
30 November–6 December 2020 3,338 2,425 +38% 15.3 °C
23–29 November 2020 3,298 2,390 +38% 15.9 °C
6–12 December 2021 3,344 2,443 +37% 15.7 °C
25–31 July 2022 3,222 2,370 +36% 35.2 °C
28 June–4 July 2021 3,154 2,359 +34% 35.5 °C
13–19 December 2021 3,293 2,504 +32% 9.8 °C
22–28 November 2021 3,174 2,404 +32% 17.3 °C
29 November–5 December 2021 3,177 2,409 +32% 16.4 °C

4 of the ten are summer weeks, among them the worst of all, 2–8 August 2021: 3,895 people died, 61% more than expected, while Athens averaged 38.6 °C at the hottest hour of each day. The other 6 are weeks of November 2020, November 2021, December 2021, when the waves of the pandemic filled the hospitals.

4. Does the heat kill too?

Yes. Every dot of the chart is a week of June to September since 2015: how hot it was in Athens, where more than a third of the people of Greece live, and how many more people died in all of Greece than expected.

Code 
summer<-weekly[weekly$week>=23&weekly$week<=39&!is.na(weekly$tmax),]
summer$hover<-paste0(week_dates(summer$monday),": ",format(round(summer$tmax,1),nsmall=1),
                     " °C, deaths ",percent(summer$percent,sign=TRUE))
summer$hot<-summer$tmax>=36
plot_ly(summer[!summer$hot,],x=~tmax,y=~percent,type="scatter",mode="markers",
        name="Other summer weeks",marker=list(color=gray,size=8,opacity=0.7),hovertext=~hover,
        hovertemplate="%{hovertext}<extra></extra>") %>%
  add_trace(data=summer[summer$hot,],name="Weeks of 36 °C or more",
            marker=list(color=greek_red,size=10,opacity=1)) %>%
  chart("Summer weeks: heat in Athens and deaths in Greece",
        paste("Eurostat, demo_r_mwk_ts; ERA5-Land through Open-Meteo. Weeks 23 to 39 of each",
              "year (June to September)."),"Deaths above the expected, %",
        x_axis=list(title="Average of the highest temperatures of the week in Athens, °C"),
        legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=110),note_y=-0.22)

Interactive chart: Summer weeks: heat in Athens and deaths in Greece

Code 
summer$band<-cut(summer$tmax,c(-Inf,30,33,36,Inf),right=FALSE,
                 labels=c("Under 30 °C","30 to 33 °C","33 to 36 °C","36 °C or more"))
bands<-aggregate(percent~band,summer,mean)
bands$weeks<-as.vector(table(summer$band)[as.character(bands$band)])
knitr::kable(data.frame(band=bands$band,weeks=bands$weeks,
                        excess=percent(bands$percent,1,sign=TRUE)),
             col.names=c("Athens, average highest temperature of the week","Weeks",
                         "Deaths above the expected, on average"),align="lrr")
Athens, average highest temperature of the week Weeks Deaths above the expected, on average
Under 30 °C 47 +0.3%
30 to 33 °C 81 +0.6%
33 to 36 °C 54 +6.5%
36 °C or more 10 +22.4%

In the summer weeks under 33 °C, about as many people died as expected. In the 10 weeks of 36 °C or more, 22% more died than expected, on average. Heat strains the heart and the lungs, most of all in old and sick people (see Athens Is Getting Hotter). Not every hot week was deadly, though: in the hottest week of all, 21–27 July 2025 at 38.7 °C, deaths were +1% against the expected.

5. Who died?

The same model, fitted to each age group, gives the excess deaths of 2020–2022 by age. The youngest groups are put together, as they have few deaths.

Code 
groups<-list(`Under 40`=c("Y_LT10","Y10-19","Y20-29","Y30-39"),`40–49`="Y40-49",
             `50–59`="Y50-59",`60–69`="Y60-69",`70–79`="Y70-79",`80–89`="Y80-89",
             `90 and over`="Y_GE90")
ages<-do.call(rbind,lapply(names(groups),function(group) {
  parts<-lapply(groups[[group]],function(code) {
    x<-by_age[by_age$age==code,c("time","values")]
    names(x)[2]<-"deaths"
    x$year<-as.integer(substr(x$time,1,4))
    x$week<-as.integer(substr(x$time,7,8))
    expect(x)$weeks
  })
  y<-do.call(rbind,parts)
  y<-y[y$year%in%2020:2022,]
  data.frame(age=group,deaths=sum(y$deaths),expected=sum(y$expected))
}))
ages$excess<-ages$deaths-ages$expected
ages$percent<-100*ages$excess/ages$expected
ages$age<-factor(ages$age,levels=ages$age)
plot_ly(ages,x=~age,y=~percent,type="bar",marker=list(color=greek_red),
        text=~number(excess),textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE,
        hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f}% above the expected<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("Deaths above the expected by age, 2020–2022, %",
        "Eurostat, demo_r_mwk_10; the model above, for each group. On the bars: the excess deaths.",
        "% above the expected")

Interactive chart: Deaths above the expected by age, 2020–2022, %

In numbers, most of the excess deaths were of old people: 25,775 of the 35,606 were of people aged 70 or more. But against what was expected for each age, the pandemic years hit people aged 60 to 79 hardest (+18%), more than those aged 80 or more (+6%), whose deaths are many in any year. The groups add up to a little less than the total of question 2, as each group has a model of its own and a few deaths have no age.

6. How does Greece compare with the EU?

Eurostat publishes its own measure for every country: the deaths of each month against the average of the same month in 2016–2019. It has no trend for the ageing of the population, so it counts a little more excess than the model above. Averaged over the 36 months of 2020–2022:

Code 
eu_name<-c(setNames(eu_countries$name,eu_countries$code),EU27_2020="EU-27")
months_2020_2022<-eurostat_excess[eurostat_excess$time>="2020-01"&eurostat_excess$time<="2022-12"&
                                    eurostat_excess$geo%in%names(eu_name),]
eu<-aggregate(values~geo,months_2020_2022,mean)
eu$name<-eu_name[eu$geo]
eu<-eu[order(eu$values),]
countries<-eu[eu$geo!="EU27_2020",]
greece_rank<-match("EL",rev(countries$geo))
plot_ly(eu,x=~values,y=~factor(name,levels=name),type="bar",orientation="h",
        marker=list(color=ifelse(eu$geo=="EL",greek_red,ifelse(eu$geo=="EU27_2020",blue,gray))),
        text=~percent(values,1),textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE,
        hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x:.1f}% more deaths than in 2016–2019<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("Deaths above 2016–2019, average month of 2020–2022, %",
        "Eurostat, demo_mexrt: the deaths of each month against the average of 2016–2019",
        margin=list(l=130,t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.08)

Interactive chart: Deaths above 2016–2019, average month of 2020–2022, %

About average. With 13.6% more deaths a month than in 2016–2019, Greece was 10th of the 27 countries, against 13.3% for the EU as a whole. Bulgaria had the most, Sweden the fewest.

7. What came after the pandemic?

In 2025, 121,566 people died in Greece, against 121,669 in an average year of 2016–2019: about as many, although the population is older. Eurostat’s measure, which compares each month with 2016–2019 and has no trend, averaged -0.1% for Greece in 2025. The model above expects the deaths to grow by 0.8% a year as the population ages, so it counts 7,646 deaths fewer than expected (-5.9%).

Code 
recent<-eurostat_excess[eurostat_excess$geo%in%c("EL","EU27_2020"),]
recent$date<-as.Date(paste0(recent$time,"-01"))
recent<-recent[order(recent$date),]
plot_ly(recent[recent$geo=="EL",],x=~date,y=~values,type="scatter",mode="lines",name="Greece",
        line=list(color=greek_red,width=2),hovertemplate="Greece: %{y:.1f}%<extra></extra>") %>%
  add_trace(data=recent[recent$geo=="EU27_2020",],name="EU-27",line=list(color=blue,width=2),
            hovertemplate="EU-27: %{y:.1f}%<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("Deaths of each month against 2016–2019, %",
        paste0("Eurostat, demo_mexrt, January 2020 to ",
               format(max(recent$date),"%B %Y")),"% above (+) or below (−)",
        hovermode="x unified",legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90))

Interactive chart: Deaths of each month against 2016–2019, %

Two things can keep the deaths of the years after a pandemic below the trend:

  • Some of the deaths came early. The pandemic and the heatwaves took the lives of many people who were already very old or very ill. Some of them would have died in the years that followed; as they died earlier, fewer people die in those years. Demographers call this mortality displacement.
  • The trend of 2015–2019 may not hold. The model lets the expected deaths grow by 0.8% a year, as they did before the pandemic. If people now live longer than that trend assumes, the expected deaths are too high, and part of the gap is the model’s error, not fewer deaths.

Sources

  • Eurostat: demo_r_mwk_ts (deaths by week), demo_r_mwk_10 (deaths by week and ten-year age group), demo_mexrt (excess mortality by month).
  • Temperatures: ERA5-Land (Muñoz-Sabater et al. 2021), through the historical weather API of Open-Meteo (Zippenfenig 2023), for the point of the grid nearest to the centre of Athens.
