item.title: From Lignite to Sunshine: How Greece Makes Its Electricity
item.description: Greek electricity in Eurostat data since 1990: how lignite gave way to gas, sun and wind, what changes with the seasons, how Greece compares with the EU, what households pay, and how Greece began to sell electricity abroad.
item.content:encoded:
Greek electricity in Eurostat data since 1990: how lignite gave way to gas, sun and wind, what changes with the seasons, how Greece compares with the EU, what households pay, and how Greece began to sell electricity abroad.

What is this?

For most of the last century Greece made its electricity by burning lignite, a soft brown coal dug from open-pit mines around Ptolemaida and Kozani in Western Macedonia and around Megalopoli in the Peloponnese. Today most of it comes from natural gas, the sun and the wind. This story follows the change with official data, in six questions:

  1. What does Greece make its electricity from?
  2. When did the sun and the wind overtake lignite?
  3. What changes with the seasons?
  4. How does Greece compare with the rest of the EU?
  5. What do households pay?
  6. Does Greece now sell electricity abroad?

All the data come from Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU. They are downloaded when the page is rendered, so a new render brings in the latest figures. Electricity is counted in terawatt hours (TWh), a billion kilowatt hours each, or in gigawatt hours (GWh), a million kilowatt hours each.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("eurostat","plotly"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values; the time as text: "2024", "2024-05", "2024-S1"
eurostat_values<-function(id,filters) {
  x<-get_eurostat(id,filters=filters,time_format="raw",cache=FALSE)
  result<-as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values),])
  result$time<-as.character(result$time)
  return(result)
}
# the fuels of the charts, in the order of the stack, with their codes in the yearly and the monthly
# data, and colours that colour-blind readers can also tell apart. The solid fuel of Greece is
# lignite
fuels<-data.frame(fuel=c("Lignite","Oil","Natural gas","Hydro","Wind","Solar"),
                  yearly=c("C0000X0350-0370","O4000XBIO","G3000","RA100","RA300","RA420"),
                  monthly=c("C0000","O4000XBIO","G3000","RA100","RA300","RA400"),
                  color=c("#8f5a12","#8e6bb8","#d1495b","#1f5f99","#4aa3df","#d29a00"))
# production by fuel, one column for each fuel and the rest (biomass, waste) as "Other", GWh
by_fuel<-function(x,codes) {
  times<-sort(unique(x$time))
  result<-data.frame(time=times)
  for(k in seq_along(codes)) {
    s<-x[x$siec==codes[k],]
    result[[fuels$fuel[k]]]<-s$values[match(times,s$time)]
  }
  total<-x[x$siec=="TOTAL",]
  result$total<-total$values[match(times,total$time)]
  result$Other<-result$total-rowSums(result[fuels$fuel],na.rm=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
# gross production of electricity in Greece by fuel, every year since 1990, TWh
production<-eurostat_values("nrg_bal_peh",list(geo="EL",nrg_bal="GEP",unit="GWH",
                                              siec=c("TOTAL",fuels$yearly)))
yearly<-by_fuel(production,fuels$yearly)
yearly$year<-as.integer(yearly$time)
columns<-c(fuels$fuel,"Other","total")
yearly[columns]<-yearly[columns]/1000
last<-max(yearly$year)
# the share of each fuel in the production of each year, %
shares<-cbind(year=yearly$year,100*yearly[c(fuels$fuel,"Other")]/yearly$total)
shares$sun_wind<-shares$Wind+shares$Solar
at<-function(column,year,x=shares) {
  result<-x[[column]][x$year==year]
  return(result)
}
# the first year in which the sun and the wind made more than lignite
crossing<-min(shares$year[shares$sun_wind>shares$Lignite])
# net production by fuel every month since January 2017, when the monthly data first split lignite,
# gas and the sun, GWh
monthly<-eurostat_values("nrg_cb_pem",list(geo="EL",unit="GWH",siec=c("TOTAL",fuels$monthly)))
monthly<-by_fuel(monthly[monthly$time>="2017-01",],fuels$monthly)
monthly$year<-as.integer(substr(monthly$time,1,4))
monthly$month<-as.integer(substr(monthly$time,6,7))
monthly$sun_wind<-100*(monthly$Wind+monthly$Solar)/monthly$total
latest_month<-monthly$time[nrow(monthly)]
# the last three years with all twelve months
full_years<-as.integer(names(which(table(monthly$year)==12)))
recent_years<-tail(full_years,3)
recent<-monthly[monthly$year%in%recent_years,]
# their average month: the share of the sun and the wind, the production and the gas
sun_wind_month<-tapply(recent$sun_wind,recent$month,mean)
monthly_total<-tapply(recent$total,recent$month,mean)
monthly_gas<-tapply(recent[["Natural gas"]],recent$month,mean)
best<-which.max(sun_wind_month)
worst<-which.min(sun_wind_month)
peak<-which.max(monthly_total)
low<-which.min(monthly_total)
season<-rep(c("winter","spring","summer","autumn","winter"),c(2,3,3,3,1))
# the share of renewables in the electricity that each country consumes, %, as the EU counts it for
# its targets. Its newest year is provisional at first (flag "p"), so the comparison uses the last
# year that Greece has a final figure for
renewables<-as.data.frame(get_eurostat("nrg_ind_ren",time_format="raw",cache=FALSE,
                                       keepFlags=TRUE))
renewables$year<-as.integer(as.character(renewables[[intersect(c("time","TIME_PERIOD"),
                                                               names(renewables))[1]]]))
renewables<-renewables[renewables$nrg_bal=="REN_ELC"&!is.na(renewables$values),]
final<-is.na(renewables$flags)|renewables$flags==""
greece_renewables<-renewables[renewables$geo=="EL",]
ren_year<-max(greece_renewables$year[final[renewables$geo=="EL"]])
ren_latest<-max(greece_renewables$year)
eu_name<-c(setNames(eu_countries$name,eu_countries$code),EU27_2020="EU-27")
eu_renewables<-renewables[renewables$year==ren_year&renewables$geo%in%names(eu_name),]
eu_renewables$name<-eu_name[eu_renewables$geo]
eu_renewables<-eu_renewables[order(-eu_renewables$values),]
ren_at<-function(geo,year) {
  result<-renewables$values[renewables$geo==geo&renewables$year==year]
  return(result)
}
# what households pay for a kilowatt hour, euros with all taxes, in Eurostat's middle band of
# 2,500 to 5,000 kWh a year, every half year since 2007
prices<-eurostat_values("nrg_pc_204",list(geo=c("EL","EU27_2020"),nrg_cons="KWH2500-4999",
                                         tax="I_TAX",currency="EUR",unit="KWH"))
# a half year as the day it starts: 2024-S2 is 1 July 2024
prices$date<-as.Date(paste0(substr(prices$time,1,4),
                            ifelse(substr(prices$time,7,7)=="1","-01-01","-07-01")))
prices<-prices[order(prices$date),]
both<-merge(prices[prices$geo=="EL",c("time","date","values")],
            prices[prices$geo=="EU27_2020",c("time","values")],by="time",
            suffixes=c("_greece","_eu"))
both<-both[order(both$date),]
# the dearest half year of the energy crisis in Greece
crisis<-both[both$date>=as.Date("2021-01-01")&both$date<=as.Date("2023-07-01"),]
crisis<-crisis[order(-crisis$values_greece),]
# electricity bought from and sold to other countries, every year since 1990, TWh
trade<-eurostat_values("nrg_cb_e",list(geo="EL",siec="E7000",unit="GWH",nrg_bal=c("IMP","EXP")))
trade<-reshape(trade[,c("nrg_bal","time","values")],idvar="time",timevar="nrg_bal",
               direction="wide")
trade<-data.frame(year=as.integer(trade$time),imports=trade$values.IMP/1000,
                  exports=trade$values.EXP/1000)
trade<-trade[order(trade$year),]
trade$net<-trade$exports-trade$imports
trade_last<-max(trade$year)
# the years of the latest run of years in which Greece sold more than it bought, and the year
# before them in which it last did so
last_import<-max(trade$year[trade$net<=0])
first_export<-last_import+1
earlier_export<-trade$year[trade$net>0&trade$year<last_import]
Code 
greek_red<-"#d62728"
blue<-"#1f77b4"
gray<-"#9e9e9e"
dark_gray<-"#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes and the labels
# a scale from a small share (white) to a large one (dark blue)
blues<-list(c(0,"#f4f8fd"),c(0.5,"#3987e5"),c(1,"#0d366b"))
# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(),
                margin=list(t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.16,...) {
  note<-list(text=paste("Source:",source),xref="paper",yref="paper",x=0,y=note_y,xanchor="left",
             yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=11,color=dark_gray))
  result<-layout(p,
                 title=list(text=title,x=0.02,xanchor="left",y=0.97,yanchor="top"),
                 yaxis=c(list(title=y_title),y_axis),
                 xaxis=c(list(title=""),x_axis),
                 margin=margin,
                 annotations=c(annotations,list(note)),
                 ...) %>%
    config(displaylogo=FALSE)
  return(result)
}
legend_top<-list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.02,yanchor="bottom")
months<-factor(month.abb,levels=month.abb) # in this order on an axis
# labels just right of the plot, at the given heights, moved apart where they would touch
spread<-function(y,gap) {
  o<-order(y)
  for(k in seq_along(o)[-1])
    y[o[k]]<-max(y[o[k]],y[o[k-1]]+gap)
  return(y)
}
right_labels<-function(y,text) {
  result<-lapply(seq_along(y),function(k) {
    list(x=1.01,y=y[k],text=text[k],xref="paper",yref="y",xanchor="left",showarrow=FALSE,
         font=list(size=12,color=dark_gray))
  })
  return(result)
}
# short labels of numbers
twh<-function(x) {
  result<-paste(format(round(x,1),nsmall=1,trim=TRUE),"TWh")
  return(result)
}
percent<-function(x,digits=0) {
  result<-paste0(format(round(x,digits),nsmall=digits,trim=TRUE),"%")
  return(result)
}
gwh<-function(x) {
  result<-paste(format(round(x),big.mark=",",trim=TRUE),"GWh")
  return(result)
}
euro<-function(x) {
  result<-paste0("€",format(round(x,3),nsmall=3,trim=TRUE))
  return(result)
}
month_label<-function(time) {
  result<-paste(month.name[as.integer(substr(time,6,7))],substr(time,1,4))
  return(result)
}
# a half year in words: "2024-S2" is "the second half of 2024"
half<-function(time) {
  result<-paste(ifelse(substr(time,7,7)=="1","the first half of","the second half of"),
                substr(time,1,4))
  return(result)
}
ordinal<-function(n) {
  suffix<-ifelse(n%%100%in%11:13,"th",c("th","st","nd","rd",rep("th",6))[n%%10+1])
  result<-paste0(n,suffix)
  return(result)
}

1. What does Greece make its electricity from?

Mostly from natural gas, the sun and the wind; hardly any more from lignite. In 2024 Greece produced 57.9 TWh of electricity. Natural gas made 37% of it, the wind 21%, the sun 19% and lignite 6%. In 1990 lignite had made 72%, and the sun and the wind nothing at all.

Code 
stack<-data.frame(fuel=c(fuels$fuel,"Other"),color=c(fuels$color,gray))
p<-plot_ly()
for(k in seq_len(nrow(stack))) {
  band<-data.frame(year=yearly$year,twh=yearly[[stack$fuel[k]]])
  p<-p %>%
    add_trace(data=band,x=~year,y=~twh,type="scatter",mode="lines",stackgroup="one",
              name=stack$fuel[k],fillcolor=stack$color[k],
              line=list(color=stack$color[k],width=0.5),
              hovertemplate=paste0(stack$fuel[k],": %{y:.1f} TWh<extra></extra>"))
}
# the name of each fuel next to its band in the last year
top<-cumsum(unlist(yearly[yearly$year==last,stack$fuel]))
middle<-top-unlist(yearly[yearly$year==last,stack$fuel])/2
p %>%
  chart("Greek electricity by fuel, TWh a year",
        paste0("Eurostat, nrg_bal_peh, gross production, 1990–",last,
               ". Other: biomass, biogas and waste."),"TWh",
        annotations=right_labels(spread(middle,0.07*max(yearly$total)),stack$fuel),
        hovermode="x unified",showlegend=FALSE,margin=list(t=70,b=90,r=110),
        x_axis=list(range=c(1990,last)))

The same years as shares of the production:

mix<-shares[shares$year%in%table_years,c("year",fuels$fuel,"Other")]

2000 64% 17% 11% 7% 1% 0% 1%
2010 54% 11% 17% 13% 5% 0% 1%
2019 25% 11% 30% 8% 15% 9% 2%
2024 6% 8% 37% 6% 21% 19% 2%

2. When did the sun and the wind overtake lignite?

In 2020. That year the sun and the wind made 29% of the electricity of Greece, lignite 14%. Lignite had made 73% in 1994; by 2024 it was down to 6%. Natural gas, which hardly made any electricity in 1990, took over much of the rest: it now makes 37%, and almost all of that gas comes from abroad, by pipeline and by ship.

Code 
lines<-data.frame(series=c("Lignite","Natural gas","Sun and wind"),
                  column=c("Lignite","Natural gas","sun_wind"),
                  color=c(fuels$color[1],fuels$color[3],fuels$color[6]))
p<-plot_ly()
for(k in seq_len(nrow(lines))) {
  line<-data.frame(year=shares$year,share=shares[[lines$column[k]]])
  p<-p %>%
    add_trace(data=line,x=~year,y=~share,type="scatter",mode="lines",name=lines$series[k],
              line=list(color=lines$color[k],width=2),
              hovertemplate=paste0(lines$series[k],": %{y:.1f}%<extra></extra>"))
}
ends<-sapply(lines$column,function(column) at(column,last))
p %>%
  chart("Share of Greek electricity, %",
        paste0("Eurostat, nrg_bal_peh, gross production, 1990–",last),"% of production",
        annotations=c(right_labels(spread(ends,6),lines$series),
                      list(list(x=crossing,y=at("sun_wind",crossing),
                                text=paste0(crossing,": the sun and the wind<br>overtake lignite"),
                                showarrow=TRUE,ax=-180,ay=-10,arrowcolor=dark_gray,
                                font=list(size=12,color=dark_gray)))),
        hovermode="x unified",showlegend=FALSE,margin=list(t=70,b=90,r=110),
        x_axis=list(range=c(1990,last)),y_axis=list(range=c(0,100)))

Interactive chart: Share of Greek electricity, %

3. What changes with the seasons?

The sun and the wind make the largest share in spring, when there is plenty of both and little need for heating or cooling. In 2023–2025 they made on average 47% of the electricity of April, but 33% of December. Their best month so far was October 2022, with 53%.

The monthly figures are net production and Eurostat’s first estimates, so they do not add up exactly to the yearly ones above.

Code 
z<-tapply(monthly$sun_wind,list(monthly$year,monthly$month),mean)
plot_ly(x=months,y=rownames(z),z=z,type="heatmap",colorscale=blues,zmin=0,
        zmax=max(monthly$sun_wind),xgap=2,ygap=2,
        colorbar=list(title=list(text="% from sun<br>and wind"),thickness=12),
        hovertemplate="%{x} %{y}: %{z:.0f}% from the sun and the wind<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("Sun and wind, % of each month",
        paste0("Eurostat, nrg_cb_pem, net production, January 2017 to ",month_label(latest_month),
               "; blank: no data yet"),
        y_axis=list(type="category",autorange="reversed"),note_y=-0.1)

Interactive chart: Sun and wind, % of each month

The rest comes mostly from gas, and gas also follows the demand. Greece uses the most electricity in summer, for air conditioning (see Athens Is Getting Hotter), and in winter. In an average July it produced 5,515 GWh, 2,159 GWh more than in an average April, and gas made 1,122 GWh of the difference.

Code 
average<-aggregate(recent[c(fuels$fuel,"Other")],list(month=recent$month),mean)
p<-plot_ly()
for(k in seq_len(nrow(stack))) {
  bars<-data.frame(month=months[average$month],gwh=average[[stack$fuel[k]]])
  p<-p %>%
    add_trace(data=bars,x=~month,y=~gwh,type="bar",name=stack$fuel[k],
              marker=list(color=stack$color[k],line=list(color="white",width=1)),
              hovertemplate=paste0(stack$fuel[k],": %{y:,.0f} GWh<extra></extra>"))
}
p %>%
  chart("An average month by fuel, GWh",
        paste0("Eurostat, nrg_cb_pem, net production, the average of ",
               paste(range(recent_years),collapse="–"),". Other: biomass, biogas and waste."),"GWh",
        barmode="stack",bargap=0.15,hovermode="x unified",
        legend=c(legend_top,traceorder="normal"),margin=list(t=100,b=90))

Interactive chart: An average month by fuel, GWh

4. How does Greece compare with the rest of the EU?

The EU sets its targets with another measure: the share of renewable energy in the electricity a country consumes, counting hydro and biomass as well as the sun and the wind, and averaging hydro and wind over several years so that one wet or windy year does not count too much. On that measure Greece went from 7.8% in 2004 to 51.2% in 2024, 10th of the 27 countries of the EU and above its average of 47.5%. Eurostat’s first, provisional figure for 2025 is 60.9%.

Code 
eu_renewables<-eu_renewables[order(eu_renewables$values),]
bar_colors<-ifelse(eu_renewables$geo=="EL",greek_red,
                   ifelse(eu_renewables$geo=="EU27_2020",blue,gray))
plot_ly(eu_renewables,x=~values,y=~factor(name,levels=name),type="bar",orientation="h",
        marker=list(color=bar_colors),text=~percent(values),textposition="outside",
        cliponaxis=FALSE,hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x:.1f}%<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Renewable electricity in the EU, ",ren_year,", %"),
        paste("Eurostat, nrg_ind_ren (REN_ELC):",
              "the share of renewable energy in gross electricity consumption"),
        x_axis=list(range=c(0,105)),margin=list(l=130,t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.08)

Interactive chart: Renewable electricity in the EU, 2024, %

5. What do households pay?

Less than the average household of the EU, in every half year since 2007. In the energy crisis of 2021–2023, sharpened by the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the price of a kilowatt hour for a Greek household rose to €0.244 in the second half of 2022 (with all taxes, in the middle band of 2,500 to 5,000 kWh a year), against €0.277 in the EU. In the first half of 2026 it was €0.240, against €0.283.

Code 
plot_ly(both,x=~date,y=~values_greece,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers",name="Greece",
        line=list(color=greek_red,width=2),marker=list(color=greek_red,size=8),
        hovertemplate="Greece: €%{y:.3f}<extra></extra>") %>%
  add_trace(y=~values_eu,name="EU-27",line=list(color=blue,width=2),
            marker=list(color=blue,size=8),hovertemplate="EU-27: €%{y:.3f}<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("Price of a kilowatt hour for households, euros",
        paste("Eurostat, nrg_pc_204, with all taxes, for households using 2,500 to 5,000 kWh a",
              "year, every half year"),
        "Euros per kWh",y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero"),hovermode="x unified",
        legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90))

Interactive chart: Price of a kilowatt hour for households, euros

6. Does Greece now sell electricity abroad?

Yes, since 2024. For three decades Greece bought more electricity from its neighbours than it sold them: in 2019 it bought 9.9 TWh more than it sold. In 2024 it sold more than it bought, for the first time since 2000, and in 2025 it sold 3.0 TWh more: 6.4 TWh went abroad and 3.4 TWh came in.

Code 
trade$hover<-paste0(trade$year,": sold ",twh(trade$exports),", bought ",twh(trade$imports))
plot_ly(trade,x=~year,y=~net,type="bar",marker=list(color=ifelse(trade$net>0,greek_red,gray)),
        hovertext=~hover,hovertemplate="%{hovertext}<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("Sold abroad minus bought, TWh a year",
        paste0("Eurostat, nrg_cb_e, 1990–",trade_last,
               ". Below zero: Greece bought more than it sold."),
        "TWh")

Interactive chart: Sold abroad minus bought, TWh a year

item.title: Where the Earth Erupts: Volcanoes of the World
item.description: Where the world’s volcanoes are, which ones erupt, how big the eruptions get, the deadliest eruptions on record, how many people live close to a volcano, and where Greece stands.
item.content:encoded:
Where the world’s volcanoes are, which ones erupt, how big the eruptions get, the deadliest eruptions on record, how many people live close to a volcano, and where Greece stands.

What is this?

Most people know a few volcanoes: Vesuvius, Etna, Krakatau, perhaps Santorini. They are a small part of the whole. More than a thousand volcanoes have erupted in the last 10,000 years, and some of them erupt again every year. This story asks five questions:

  1. Where in the world are the volcanoes?
  2. Which volcanoes erupt, and how often?
  3. How big do eruptions get?
  4. Which were the deadliest eruptions?
  5. How many people live close to a volcano, and where does Greece stand?

Where the Earth Shakes looks at earthquakes, Waves from the Sea at tsunamis, and Natural Disasters puts the hazards side by side.

The data come from two sources, downloaded when the page is rendered:

  • The Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program (GVP), which keeps the Volcanoes of the World database, no key needed (GVP): the list of volcanoes that have erupted in the Holocene (the last 10,000 years or so), where they are and what kind they are; their eruptions, with the year they began and how explosive they were; and the number of people who live within 5, 10, 30 and 100 kilometres of each volcano.
  • NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), whose Significant Volcanic Eruptions Database lists the eruptions that did the most harm, with the number of deaths where it is known (NCEI volcanoes).

The map also draws the boundaries between the plates of the Earth’s crust, from Peter Bird’s model (Bird 2003), in the version of the GitHub repository fraxen/tectonicplates.

The Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) measures how big an explosive eruption was, on a scale that starts at 0 for a gentle eruption and is open-ended, with 8 for the largest eruptions in history. It is mainly based on the volume of ash thrown out, and also on the height of the eruption cloud. Each step up is about ten times more ash, apart from the first (USGS; Newhall and Self 1982).

A volcano here is a volcano of the GVP’s list. A large volcanic field, with hundreds of small vents, counts as one volcano.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("plotly", "jsonlite"))
library(plotly)
library(jsonlite)

The data

Code 
# the layers of the GVP's web service, as tables
gvp<-function(layer) {
  result<-read.csv(paste0("https://webservices.volcano.si.edu/geoserver/GVP-VOTW/ows?service=WFS",
                          "&version=2.0.0&request=GetFeature&typeName=GVP-VOTW:",layer,
                          "&outputFormat=csv"),encoding="UTF-8")
  return(result)
}
# the volcanoes of the Holocene: place, type, tectonic setting and last eruption
volcanoes<-gvp("Smithsonian_VOTW_Holocene_Volcanoes")
# the eruptions of the Holocene: one row for each eruption, with the year it began and its VEI
eruptions<-gvp("Smithsonian_VOTW_Holocene_Eruptions")
# the people who live within 5, 10, 30 and 100 km of each volcano
people<-gvp("E3WebApp_HoloceneVolcanoes")
# NOAA's significant eruptions: 200 to a page
noaa_page<-function(page) {
  result<-fromJSON(paste0("https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/hazel/hazard-service/api/v1/volcanoes",
                          "?page=",page))
  return(result)
}
first_page<-noaa_page(1)
pages<-c(list(first_page$items),
         lapply(seq_len(first_page$totalPages)[-1],function(page) noaa_page(page)$items))
# the pages as one table: a column that a page lacks is empty there
columns<-unique(unlist(lapply(pages,names)))
significant<-do.call(rbind,lapply(pages,function(x) {
  x[setdiff(columns,names(x))]<-NA
  x[columns]
}))
# the boundaries of the plates (Bird 2003), as lines
plates<-fromJSON(paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fraxen/tectonicplates/master/",
                        "GeoJSON/PB2002_boundaries.json"),simplifyVector=FALSE)

# the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(),
                margin=list(t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.16,...) {
  note<-list(text=paste("Source:",source),xref="paper",yref="paper",x=0,y=note_y,xanchor="left",
             yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=11,color=dark_gray))

# numbers in the text
number<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x),big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE,trim=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
percent<-function(x,digits=0) {
  result<-paste0(format(round(x,digits),nsmall=digits,trim=TRUE),"%")
  return(result)
}
one<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x,1),nsmall=1,trim=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
two<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x,2),nsmall=2,trim=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
# millions of people: one decimal below 10 million
million<-function(x) {
  result<-ifelse(abs(x)>=1e7,number(x/1e6),one(x/1e6))
  return(result)
}
and_list<-function(x) {
  if(length(x)<2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  result<-paste(paste(head(x,-1),collapse=", "),"and",tail(x,1))
  return(result)
}
# country names that take "the" in a sentence
with_the<-function(x) {
  result<-ifelse(x%in%c("United States","United Kingdom"),paste("the",x),x)
  return(result)
}
# the first letter of a sentence in capitals
cap<-function(x) {
  result<-paste0(toupper(substr(x,1,1)),substring(x,2))

Greece has 5 volcanoes in the list: Santorini (last eruption 1950), Nisyros (last eruption 1888), Kolumbo (last eruption 1650), Milos (last eruption 140) and Methana (last eruption 258 BCE). That is far fewer than Italy’s 13 or Iceland’s 35.

greece_eruptions<-confirmed[confirmed$country%in%"Greece",]
santorini_eruptions<-greece_eruptions[greece_eruptions$Volcano_Name=="Santorini",]
minoan<-santorini_eruptions[which.max(santorini_eruptions$ExplosivityIndexMax),]
last_santorini<-max(santorini_eruptions$StartDateYear)

kolumbo_dead<-sum(kolumbo$dead,na.rm=TRUE)
santorini_dead<-with_deaths[with_deaths$name=="Santorini",]

Santorini’s recent eruptions were small, but its largest was far older. The GVP lists 11 confirmed eruptions of Santorini in the Holocene, the last in 1950, with a VEI of 2; the largest, dated to 1610 BCE, was VEI 7, one of the 7 of VEI 7 or more in the Holocene in the list. Kolumbo, whose summit is 18 metres below the sea, erupted in 1650 (VEI 4), and NOAA’s database gives its 4 entries of that year 140 deaths together. Within 30 km of Santorini live 12,336 people, and within 100 km 67,468. Of the 4 volcanoes with a population count, the most people live near Methana (48,917 within 30 km). By the same measure Campi Flegrei, in Italy, has 3.0 million.

So, what does it mean?

  1. Volcanoes are where the plates meet, and in a few countries. The 10 countries with the most volcanoes have 59% of the 1,209 in the list, and 69% sit in subduction zones. The United States, Japan and Indonesia lead.
  2. About 34 eruptions begin a year, and the number has not changed since 1960. The apparent rise before that is a rise in what was recorded.
  3. Most eruptions are small. 83% of the eruptions since 1960 are VEI 0 to 2; 5 since 1800 were VEI 6 or more.
  4. The deadliest eruptions are not always the biggest. The five deadliest on record have 53% of the deaths of the eruptions with a known number, Tambora 1815, Krakatau 1883, Ilopango 450, Pelee 1902 and Nevado del Ruiz 1985.
  5. Many volcanoes have people near them. In 76 volcanoes of the list, more than a million people live within 30 km; Greece has 5 volcanoes in the list, and Santorini is the one that erupted last.

What this does not show. A list of eruptions is a list of what people recorded: it is incomplete before about 1960, and eruptions on the seafloor are the hardest to see. The VEI measures the explosion, not the harm, and it is missing for some eruptions. NOAA lists only significant eruptions, and for many of them the deaths are not known, so the totals are minimums, and a death toll is partly a matter of who counted and how. The numbers of people near volcanoes come from a population map whose year the data do not give, and each person near several volcanoes is counted several times. Nothing here says when or where the next eruption will be: a count of past eruptions is not a forecast.

For earthquakes, see Where the Earth Shakes; for tsunamis, Waves from the Sea; for all the hazards together, Natural Disasters.

item.title: Waves from the Sea: Where Tsunamis Start and Where They Strike Since 1900
item.description: Tsunamis since 1900 in NOAA’s global database: where they start, how far their waves travel, how tall they get, which were the deadliest, and whether there are more of them than there used to be.
item.content:encoded:
Tsunamis since 1900 in NOAA’s global database: where they start, how far their waves travel, how tall they get, which were the deadliest, and whether there are more of them than there used to be.

What is this?

A tsunami is a series of waves that starts when something moves a great deal of water at once, most often an earthquake under the sea. In the open ocean the waves are low and fast. Near a coast they grow, and they can flood it. This story looks at the tsunamis of the last 125 years and asks five questions:

  1. Where in the world do tsunamis start?
  2. Where do the waves strike, and how far do they travel?
  3. How big are they, and how often does one kill?
  4. Which were the deadliest?
  5. Are there more of them than there used to be?

For the earthquakes behind most tsunamis, see Earthquakes; for those that come from eruptions, Volcanoes; for all the hazards together, Natural Disasters.

The data come from the Global Historical Tsunami Database of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), kept by its National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) (database). It lists tsunamis from 2000 BC to today, collected from reports, tide gauges and surveys. Its hazard-service interface gives it as two tables, downloaded here when the page is rendered, with no key:

  • The events: one row for each tsunami, with where its source was, what caused it, how reliable the report is, the highest water, and the deaths. We use the tsunamis since 1900, the first year of instrumentally located earthquakes (NOAA).
  • The runups: one row for each place where a tsunami’s waves were measured, with the height of the water, the distance from the source and the country. A runup is the maximum height of the water above the normal sea level (NOAA).

The meaning of every code below (validity, cause, region, kind of measurement) is from the help pages of NOAA’s own search tool (HazEL).

The record is of reports, not of every wave. A tsunami enters the database when someone saw it, measured it or wrote about it. Small waves far from people are missed, and how well they are recorded has changed over the years (section 5).

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("curl", "plotly", "jsonlite"))
library(curl)
library(plotly)
library(jsonlite)

The data

Code 
# the items of a page of NOAA's hazard service, or nothing when the request failed
noaa_items<-function(response) {
  if(is.null(response)||response$status_code!=200) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  result<-fromJSON(rawToChar(response$content))$items
  return(result)
}
# one table of NOAA's hazard service: the first page says how many pages there are, and the rest
# are asked for at the same time, five at once, because one page takes a few seconds
noaa<-function(table,filter="") {
  base<-paste0("https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/hazel/hazard-service/api/v1/tsunamis/",table,"?",filter,
               "&page=")
  first<-fromJSON(paste0(base,1))
  pages<-list("1"=first$items)
  todo<-seq_len(first$totalPages)[-1]
  for(attempt in 1:3) {
    if(length(todo)==0) break
    got<-list()
    pool<-new_pool(total_con=5,host_con=5)
    for(p in todo) {
      local({
        page<-p
        curl_fetch_multi(paste0(base,page),
                         done=function(r) got[[as.character(page)]]<<-noaa_items(r),
                         fail=function(e) NULL,pool=pool)
      })
    }
    multi_run(pool=pool)
    pages<-c(pages,got)
    todo<-setdiff(todo,as.integer(names(got)[!sapply(got,is.null)]))
  }
  stopifnot(length(todo)==0)
  # the pages in their order (they come in the order in which they are finished)
  pages<-pages[order(as.integer(names(pages)))]
  # the pages as one table: a column that a page lacks is empty there
  columns<-unique(unlist(lapply(pages,names)))
  result<-do.call(rbind,lapply(pages,function(x) {
    x[setdiff(columns,names(x))]<-NA
    x[columns]
  }))
  rownames(result)<-NULL
  return(result)
}
# the tsunamis since 1900
events_all<-noaa("events","minYear=1900&maxYear=2026")
# the places where waves were measured; this table cannot be cut by year, so all of it is downloaded
runups_all<-noaa("runups")
Code 
# the codes of NOAA (HazEL help pages)
validity<-c("-1"="erroneous entry","0"="only a seiche","1"="very doubtful","2"="questionable",
            "3"="probable","4"="definite")
# the regions of the source, in NOAA's names, and the sea or ocean that they are in
regions<-c("30"="Red Sea and Persian Gulf","40"="Black Sea and Caspian Sea",
           "50"="Mediterranean Sea","60"="Indian Ocean","70"="Southeast Atlantic",
           "71"="Southwest Atlantic","72"="Northwest Atlantic","73"="Northeast Atlantic",
           "74"="Caribbean Sea","75"="East coast of USA and Canada","76"="Gulf of Mexico",
           "77"="West coast of Africa","78"="Central Africa","80"="Hawaii",
           "81"="Australia, New Zealand and South Pacific",
           "82"="New Guinea, Solomon Is. and Vanuatu","83"="Indonesia (Pacific) and Malaysia",
           "84"="China, Koreas, Philippines, Taiwan","85"="Japan",
           "86"="Kamchatka and Kuril Islands","87"="Alaska and Aleutian Islands",
           "88"="West coast of North and Central America","89"="West coast of South America")
pacific_codes<-80:89
# the causes, in the groups of this page
cause_group<-function(code) {
  result<-rep("Other or unknown",length(code))
  result[code%in%1:3]<-"Earthquake"
  result[code%in%4:7]<-"Volcano"
  result[code%in%8]<-"Landslide"
  result[code%in%9]<-"Weather"
  return(result)
}
# the sea or ocean of a region of the source
ocean_of<-function(code) {
  result<-rep("Black, Caspian and Red Seas, Persian Gulf",length(code))
  result[code%in%70:78]<-"Atlantic Ocean, Caribbean and Gulf"
  result[code%in%50]<-"Mediterranean Sea"
  result[code%in%60]<-"Indian Ocean"
  result[code%in%pacific_codes]<-"Pacific Ocean"
  result[is.na(code)]<-NA

}

chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(),

# numbers in the text
number<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x),big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE,trim=TRUE)

}
percent<-function(x,digits=0) {

}

# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one
# without a trend
chance<-function(x,years) {
  p<-cor.test(years,x,method="kendall",exact=FALSE)$p.value
  result<-if(p<0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100*p))
  return(result)
}
Code

n_kept<-nrow(events)

}

                       events$deaths!=events$deathsTotal),]
haiti<-events[which(events$year==2010&grepl("HAITI",events$locationName)),]
n_runups_all<-nrow(runups_all)

Only probable and definite tsunamis are kept. NOAA rates every report from -1 to 4. Since 1900 the database has 1,667 entries: 860 definite, 315 probable, 221 questionable, 188 very doubtful, 22 that only caused a seiche (a wave that sloshes in a lake or bay) and 61 erroneous. This page keeps the 1,175 definite and probable ones, 70% of the entries. The rest are too uncertain to count as tsunamis. Of those kept, 75 started in a lake, a reservoir or a river rather than the sea; they stay, and are named where they matter.

Deaths are those of the tsunami alone. The database gives two figures: the deaths of the tsunami, and a total for the whole event, which includes the earthquake or eruption that caused it. For the earthquake of Haiti in 2010 the total is 316,000 and the tsunami’s own figure 7. The two differ for 47 of the tsunamis that have both, so this page uses the tsunami’s own deaths, and only where a number is recorded (section 4).

The runups are those of the kept tsunamis, in places where the report was not doubtful. The runups table has 35,150 rows for all of history, and its filters do not cut it by year, so all of it is downloaded. 31,769 are of tsunamis since 1900. Of these, 561 belong to tsunamis that are not probable or definite, and 1,127 more are marked by NOAA as doubtful, or as waves that probably came from the weather or from an eruption’s air waves rather than from the sea. That leaves 30,081 places, for 1,027 tsunamis.

Places without a position are not on the map. 73 of the kept tsunamis have no latitude and longitude, so the map shows 1,102.

The latest year is incomplete. The database has tsunamis up to 2026, a year that is not over, so the counts over time (section 5) use the 126 full years, 1900 to 2025.

1. Where in the world do tsunamis start?

Code 
# the rows of each value of x, as count() of dplyr: the values in order, a missing one last, and n
count_values<-function(x,name) {
  values<-sort(unique(x),method="radix",na.last=TRUE)
  result<-data.frame(values,vapply(values,function(v) sum(x%in%v),integer(1),USE.NAMES=FALSE))
  names(result)<-c(name,"n")
  return(result)
}
# the same, the most first
count_sorted<-function(x,name) {
  result<-count_values(x,name)
  result<-result[order(-result$n),]
  rownames(result)<-NULL
  return(result)
}
n_per_year<-sum(events$year<last_year)/n_full
by_cause<-count_values(events$cause,"cause")
by_cause$share<-100*by_cause$n/sum(by_cause$n)
by_cause$deaths<-tapply(events$deaths,events$cause,sum,na.rm=TRUE)[as.character(by_cause$cause)]
cause_n<-function(g,column="n") {

}

ocean_share<-count_values(with_region$ocean,"ocean")
ocean_share$share<-100*ocean_share$n/sum(ocean_share$n)
ocean_in<-function(g) {
  result<-ocean_share$share[ocean_share$ocean==g]

}
by_region<-count_sorted(with_region$regionCode,"regionCode")
by_region$region<-regions[as.character(by_region$regionCode)]

# the Mediterranean

The Pacific Ocean: 72% of the tsunamis. Since 1900, 1,175 probable or definite tsunamis have been recorded, 9.2 a year. By country of the source, Japan (184), United States (101), Indonesia (79), Russia (76) and Papua New Guinea (53) come first.

The Mediterranean has 96 tsunamis, 8% of the world’s. Greece has 41 of them, Italy 24 and Turkey 9. The median highest water of a Mediterranean tsunami is 1.2 m, against 0.4 m in the Pacific. The deadliest of the sea itself was in 1908, at Messina Strait, Ionian Sea, where 2,000 died. 3 of the Mediterranean entries are in lakes or reservoirs, such as the Vajont dam in Italy in 1963.

2. Where do the waves strike, and how far do they travel?

Code

far_pairs<-unique(far_runups[,c("tsunamiEventId","country")])
far_by_country<-count_sorted(far_pairs$country,"country")
far_by_country$name<-country_name(far_by_country$country)
us_pairs<-unique(far_runups[which(far_runups$country=="USA"),c("tsunamiEventId","area")])
us_far<-count_values(us_pairs$area,"area")
hawaii_far<-us_far$n[us_far$area=="HI"]
farthest<-runups[which.max(runups$distFromSource),]
runups_by_country<-count_sorted(runups$country,"country")
runups_by_country$name<-country_name(runups_by_country$country)
runups_by_country$share<-100*runups_by_country$n/sum(runups_by_country$n)

Most tsunamis stay near home; the few that cross an ocean are earthquakes of the Pacific. Of the 1,014 tsunamis with a measured distance, 27% were measured at least 1,000 km from their source, and 180 (18%) at least 3,000 km away. 93% of those 180 began in a region of the Pacific and 98% were earthquakes, with a median magnitude of 7.8. The waves that travelled farthest were those of the earthquake of 2004, measured at Baltra Island in Ecuador, 19,266 km from the source.

Code 
far_top<-head(far_by_country,10)
far_top<-far_top[order(far_top$n),]
far_top$name<-factor(far_top$name,levels=far_top$name)
plot_ly(far_top,x=~n,y=~name,type="bar",orientation="h",
        marker=list(color=ifelse(far_top$country=="USA",red,gray)),text=~n,textposition="outside",
        cliponaxis=FALSE,hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x} tsunamis<extra></extra>",showlegend=FALSE) %>%
  chart(paste0("Tsunamis that struck from ",number(far_km)," km or more"),
        "NOAA NCEI tsunami database (runups); top 10.",
        x_axis=list(showgrid=FALSE,showticklabels=FALSE,zeroline=FALSE,
                    range=c(0,1.12*max(far_top$n))),
        y_axis=list(automargin=TRUE),margin=list(l=10,t=70,b=50,r=10),note_y=-0.05)

Interactive chart: Tsunamis that struck from 3,000 km or more

The United States, mostly Hawaii, is struck from afar the most. 132 tsunamis reached the United States from 3,000 km or more, and 125 of them reached Hawaii. It lies in the middle of the Pacific, so the waves of earthquakes all round the ocean can arrive there. Then come US territories (75), Japan (58) and Canada (55).

The number of places where waves were measured says as much about the measuring as about the waves. The runups table has 11,740 places in Japan (39% of all), 4,191 in the United States and 2,458 in Indonesia. A country with few places may have few measurements rather than few waves.

3. How big are they, and how often does one kill?

Code 
with_height<-events[!is.na(events$maxWaterHeight),]
n_height<-nrow(with_height)
height_breaks<-c(0,1,3,10,30,Inf)
height_names<-c("Under 1 m","1 to 3 m","3 to 10 m","10 to 30 m","30 m or more")
with_height$class<-cut(with_height$maxWaterHeight,height_breaks,right=FALSE,labels=height_names)
height_counts<-as.integer(table(with_height$class))
height_share<-function(i) {
  result<-100*height_counts[i]/n_height
  return(result)
}
tall<-with_height[with_height$maxWaterHeight>=30,]
tallest<-with_height[which.max(with_height$maxWaterHeight),]
tall_by_cause<-table(tall$cause)
tall_slide_codes<-sum(tall$causeCode%in%c(3,5,7,8))
tall_lake<-sum(!tall$oceanicTsunami)
tall_since_2000<-sum(tall$year>=2000)
n_far_slide<-sum(far_info$cause=="Landslide")
cause_name_of<-function(code) {
  result<-c("3"="an earthquake and a landslide","8"="a landslide")[as.character(code)]
  return(result)
}
n_deadly<-sum(events$deadly,na.rm=TRUE)
n_counted<-sum(!is.na(events$deaths))
n_code_only<-sum(is.na(events$deaths)&events$deathsAmountOrder>=1,na.rm=TRUE)
n_1000<-sum(events$deathsAmountOrder==4,na.rm=TRUE)
n_100<-sum(events$deathsAmountOrder>=3,na.rm=TRUE)

More than half of the tsunamis are under a metre, and a few are over 30. Of the 998 tsunamis with a measured height of water, 56% are under 1 m, 18% 1 to 3 m, 16% 3 to 10 m, 7% 10 to 30 m and 4% (42) 30 m or more. The height is the highest water of the event above the normal sea level: for a tide gauge it is half the height from trough to crest, and for a survey the highest point reached on land (NOAA).

Code 
plot_ly(x=factor(height_names,levels=height_names),y=height_counts,type="bar",
        marker=list(color=blues),text=height_counts,textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE,
        hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y} tsunamis<extra></extra>",showlegend=FALSE) %>%
  chart("Highest water of each tsunami",
        paste0("NOAA NCEI Global Historical Tsunami Database; the ",number(n_height),
               " tsunamis with a measured height."),
        y_title="Tsunamis",y_axis=list(range=c(0,1.15*max(height_counts))),
        margin=list(t=60,b=80,r=10),note_y=-0.2)

Interactive chart: Highest water of each tsunami

The tallest waves are not those of the great earthquakes. Of the 42 tsunamis of 30 m or more, 28 were caused by a landslide alone, 6 by a volcano and 8 by an earthquake; 36 involved a landslide, 20 of them in a lake, a reservoir or a river, and 20 have happened since 2000. Of the 113 tsunamis caused by a landslide alone, 0 were measured 3,000 km or more away (section 2). The tallest of all was in SE. Alaska, AK in 1958, 524.6 m, from an earthquake and a landslide, which killed 5 people.

Most tsunamis kill nobody on record, but a few kill thousands. 165 of the 1,175 tsunamis (14%) have at least one death recorded: 1.3 a year. NOAA records a number of deaths for 156 of them, and for 9 only a class (for example “few, 1 to 50”). 41 tsunamis killed more than 100 people and 16 more than 1,000, one every 7.9 years.

4. Which were the deadliest?

Code 
dead<-events[!is.na(events$deaths),]
dead<-dead[order(-dead$deaths),]
total_dead<-sum(dead$deaths)
top10<-head(dead,10)
top2_share<-100*sum(dead$deaths[1:2])/total_dead
country_groups<-split(dead,addNA(factor(dead$country),ifany=TRUE))
by_country_dead<-do.call(rbind,lapply(country_groups,function(x) {
  data.frame(country=x$country[1],deaths=sum(x$deaths),events=nrow(x))
}))
by_country_dead<-by_country_dead[order(-by_country_dead$deaths,by_country_dead$country,
                                       method="radix"),]
rownames(by_country_dead)<-NULL
by_country_dead$name<-country_name(by_country_dead$country)
by_country_dead$share<-100*by_country_dead$deaths/total_dead
cause_phrase<-function(code) {
  result<-c("1"="Earthquake","2"="Questionable earthquake","3"="Earthquake and landslide",
            "6"="Volcano","8"="Landslide")[as.character(code)]
  return(result)
}
top10_lake<-top10[which(!top10$oceanicTsunami),]

Two tsunamis caused 83% of the deaths on record. From 1900 to 2026, 297,147 deaths are recorded, in 156 tsunamis with a number of deaths. The earthquake off Sumatra on 26 December 2004 killed 227,899 and the one off Honshu, Japan, in 2011, 18,423. Indonesia has 81% of all the recorded deaths, Japan 8%.

Code 
dc<-head(by_country_dead,8)
dc<-dc[order(dc$deaths),]
dc$name<-factor(dc$name,levels=dc$name)
plot_ly(dc,x=~deaths,y=~name,type="bar",orientation="h",
        marker=list(color=ifelse(dc$country=="INDONESIA",red,gray)),text=~number(deaths),

        "NOAA NCEI tsunami database; country of the source.",
        x_axis=list(showgrid=FALSE,showticklabels=FALSE,zeroline=FALSE,

        y_axis=list(automargin=TRUE),margin=list(l=10,t=70,b=50,r=10),note_y=-0.05)

Interactive chart: Recorded tsunami deaths by country, top 8

The ten deadliest, with the highest water that each reached:

                        place=paste0(place_name(top10$locationName),", ",

The tsunami of 1963 at Vajont Dam, Vajont River was in a reservoir, behind a dam, and not in the sea. These figures are a floor: 1,019 tsunamis have no number of deaths in the database, and the database does not say whether they had none or whether the number is unknown.

5. Are there more of them than there used to be?

Code 
# the tsunamis of each full year, and those of earthquakes of magnitude 7.5 and above
yearly<-data.frame(year=full_years,n=as.integer(table(factor(events$year,levels=full_years))))
big<-events[which(events$causeCode%in%1:3&events$eqMagnitude>=7.5&events$year<last_year),]
yearly_big<-data.frame(year=full_years,n=as.integer(table(factor(big$year,levels=full_years))))
span<-25
early<-first_year:(first_year+span-1)
late<-(last_year-span):(last_year-1)
mean_years<-function(x,years) {
  result<-mean(x$n[x$year%in%years])
  return(result)
}
decade_of<-function(x) {
  result<-10*(x%/%10)
  return(result)
}
# the same by decade, the last one not over yet
big_all<-events[which(events$causeCode%in%1:3&events$eqMagnitude>=7.5),]
decades<-sort(unique(decade_of(events$year)))
by_decade<-data.frame(decade=decades,
                      all=as.integer(table(factor(decade_of(events$year),levels=decades))),
                      big=as.integer(table(factor(decade_of(big_all$year),levels=decades))))
by_decade$label<-ifelse(by_decade$decade==decade_of(last_year),
                        paste0(by_decade$decade,"–",substr(last_year,3,4)),
                        paste0(by_decade$decade,"s"))
# how well the tsunamis are measured, by half century
half<-cut(events$year,c(1900,1950,2000,Inf),right=FALSE,
          labels=c("1900–1949","1950–1999",paste0("2000–",last_year)))
measured<-tapply(!is.na(events$maxWaterHeight),half,mean)*100

More tsunamis are recorded than a century ago, but that does not show that more happen. From 1900 to 1924 the database has 5.2 tsunamis a year; from 2001 to 2025, 17.2. A rank test over the 126 full years puts the chance of a pattern this strong without a rise at less than 1 in 100. The same holds for the tsunamis of the great earthquakes alone (magnitude 7.5 or more, 1.4 a year at first and 3.4 lately; the chance is less than 1 in 100). But the records are not equally complete: a measured height is given for 69% of the tsunamis of 1900–1949, 88% of 1950–1999 and 93% of 2000–2026. Later tsunamis are better documented, so part of the rise may be better recording. The data cannot say how much of it is real.

Code 
plot_ly(by_decade,x=~label) %>%
  add_bars(y=~all,name="All tsunamis",marker=list(color=gray),
           hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y} tsunamis<extra></extra>") %>%
  add_bars(y=~big,name="From earthquakes of magnitude 7.5+",marker=list(color=red),
           hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y} tsunamis<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("Tsunamis in each decade",
        paste0("NOAA NCEI Global Historical Tsunami Database. The ",
               by_decade$label[nrow(by_decade)]," is not over."),
        y_title="Tsunamis",legend=legend_top,barmode="group",margin=list(t=90,b=90),note_y=-0.14)

Interactive chart: Tsunamis in each decade

So, what does it mean?

  1. Tsunamis follow the earthquakes, and most of them are in the Pacific. 72% of the tsunamis with a region started in the Pacific; 77% of all of them were caused by an earthquake.
  2. A few cross an ocean. 180 tsunamis, 18% of those measured, struck 3,000 km or more from their source, and Hawaii received 125 of them.
  3. The tallest waves come from landslides, the deadliest from earthquakes. 28 of the 42 tsunamis of 30 m or more were landslides alone, and the highest water was 524.6 m.
  4. Deaths are concentrated in a few events. Two tsunamis, off Sumatra in 2004 and off Japan in 2011, account for 83% of the deaths on record.
  5. More are recorded now, and the data cannot say whether more happen. 5.2 a year at first and 17.2 lately, while the share with a measured height went from 69% to 93%.

What this does not show. The database lists the tsunamis that were reported, not all the waves of the sea, and it does not say how likely a tsunami is in any one place. The map shows the sources, not the coasts that are in danger. Doubtful reports are left out, and so is everything before 1900, though the database goes back to 2000 BC. Deaths are a floor, and the heights mix the tide gauge, the eyewitness and the survey. The numbers of places for each country depend on how well each country measures its tsunamis.

For the earthquakes behind most tsunamis, see Earthquakes; for eruptions, Volcanoes; for all the hazards together, Natural Disasters.

Sources

  • NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, NCEI/WDS Global Historical Tsunami Database, doi:10.7289/V5PN93H7: the events and the runups, from the hazard-service interface, without a key. Access is unrestricted; NOAA gives no warranty for the data (the use constraints of the dataset record).
  • NOAA NCEI, Introduction to Global Historical Tsunami Data: the definition of a runup and the notes on the data.
  • NOAA NCEI, Hazard Tsunami Search (HazEL): the help pages with the codes of validity, cause, region, deaths and kind of measurement.

item.title: Where Tornadoes Strike: The United States, Canada and What Cannot Be Compared
item.description: Where tornadoes happen: the United States state by state since 1950, how Canada’s count compares, when they strike, how strong and how deadly they are, the worst events, and whether there are more of them.
item.content:encoded:
Where tornadoes happen: the United States state by state since 1950, how Canada’s count compares, when they strike, how strong and how deadly they are, the worst events, and whether there are more of them.

What is this?

A tornado is a narrow, violently rotating column of air that reaches from a storm cloud to the ground. People think of the American Plains, and the United States does report more tornadoes than any other country we can count. But there is no single open database of the world’s tornadoes, so this story does what the data allow: it counts the United States closely, sets Canada beside it, and says plainly what cannot be compared. It asks five questions:

  1. Where do tornadoes happen?
  2. When do they strike?
  3. How strong and how deadly are they?
  4. Which were the worst?
  5. Are there more of them than there used to be?

This is one of a series on natural disasters: see the overview and Floods.

The data come from two places, downloaded when the page is rendered:

  • The United States: the tornado database of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Storm Prediction Center (SPC), one row for each tornado since 1950, with its date and time, the state, the start and end points, the length and width of its path, the rating, and the people injured and killed (SPC severe weather database). It is made of the reports that the National Weather Service’s offices send in (format description). The file used here is the one with single tracks: a tornado that crosses a state line is one row, in the state where it touched down.
  • Canada: the event summaries of the Northern Tornadoes Project, founded at Western University in 2017, which investigates tornadoes by ground, drone, aerial and satellite surveys (Northern Tornadoes Project).

The rating of a tornado is not a measurement of its wind. Since February 2007 the National Weather Service rates a tornado on the Enhanced Fujita scale, from EF0 to EF5, from the damage that it leaves: an EF0 is estimated at 65 to 85 miles per hour (the gust of three seconds), an EF1 at 86 to 110, an EF2 at 111 to 135, an EF3 at 136 to 165, an EF4 at 166 to 200 and an EF5 at more than 200 (National Weather Service). Before 2007 the original Fujita scale (F0 to F5) was used, in the same way. This page writes EF0 to EF5 for both. A tornado is rated by what it destroys, so one that crosses empty land can get a low rating whatever its wind.

Europe is missing, on purpose. The European Severe Weather Database, kept by the European Severe Storms Laboratory, lets a guest browse only recent events; the full data need a request for restricted access (ESWD). A study of its reports from 1950 to 2015 finds that tornadoes do occur in Europe, with injuries, deaths and damage, “although their reported frequencies and intensities are lower compared with the United States” (Antonescu et al. 2017). That is all this page can say about Europe from what it has read.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("plotly", "jsonlite"))
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# the SPC file of single tornado tracks since 1950, named after the last year it holds: try the
# latest years first
this_year<-as.integer(format(Sys.Date(),"%Y"))
tor<-NULL
for(y in this_year:2020) {
  tor<-tryCatch(read.csv(paste0("https://www.spc.noaa.gov/wcm/data/1950-",y,
                                "_actual_tornadoes.csv")),
                error=function(e) NULL)
  if(!is.null(tor))
    break
}
# the Northern Tornadoes Project's event summaries (Canada), a thousand rows at a time
ntp_url<-paste0("https://services.arcgis.com/rGKxabTU9mcXMw7k/arcgis/rest/services/",
                "NTP_Event_Summaries_stakeholder/FeatureServer/0/query")
ntp<-do.call(rbind,lapply(seq(0,9000,by=1000),function(offset) {
  r<-jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0(ntp_url,"?where=1%3D1&outFields=Year,event_type,province",
                               "&returnGeometry=false&resultOffset=",offset,
                               "&resultRecordCount=1000&f=json"))
  if(length(r$features)==0) NULL else r$features$attributes
}))
Code 
first_year<-min(tor$yr)
last_year<-max(tor$yr)
first_ten<-first_year:(first_year+9)
last_ten<-(last_year-9):last_year
# the rating: -9 means that the tornado has no rating
ratings<-c("EF0","EF1","EF2","EF3","EF4","EF5")

                   levels=c("Unrated",ratings))

  result<-ifelse(s%in%state.abb,state.name[match(s,state.abb)],s)

}
# the states: 50 states, with their area (the R datasets) and the census division they are in

                  state=state.name,

# the time of day: the SPC puts all times, but a few, on central standard time (3 in the column tz);
# the sun's time at the place is the clock in Greenwich (central standard time plus six hours) plus

Code

# numbers in the text
number<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x),big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE,trim=TRUE)
  return(result)
}

  result<-paste0(format(round(x,digits),nsmall=digits,trim=TRUE),"%")

}

change_text<-function(x) {
  result<-paste0(ifelse(x>=0,"+","−"),round(abs(x)),"%")
  return(result)
}
and_list<-function(x) {
  if(length(x)<2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  result<-paste(paste(head(x,-1),collapse=", "),"and",tail(x,1))
  return(result)
}
# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one
# without a trend
chance<-function(x,years) {
  p<-cor.test(years,x,method="kendall",exact=FALSE)$p.value
  result<-if(p<0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100*p))
  return(result)
}
# a date as "27 April 2011"
long_date<-function(x) {
  result<-trimws(format(as.Date(x),"%e %B %Y"))
  return(result)
}
Code 
# the unrated tornadoes in the years of the Enhanced Fujita scale, and the tornadoes that the SPC
# rated afterwards from the damage (fc = 1, from 1953 to 1982)
n_all<-nrow(tor)
unrated_years<-aggregate(cbind(share=mag<0)~yr,data=tor[tor$yr>=2007,],FUN=mean)
unrated_years$share<-100*unrated_years$share
first_unrated<-min(tor$yr[tor$mag<0&tor$yr>=2007])
rated_early<-tor[tor$fc==1,]

Some tornadoes have no rating. 1,546 of the 73,458 tornadoes (2.1%) are coded -9, “unknown”. For 1953 to 1982 the SPC has filled in an estimated rating, from the property loss and the length of the path, for 1,863 tornadoes that had none; the file marks them. The 1,546 that remain unrated come from 2007 on, and from 2019 on they are 10% to 20% of the tornadoes of a year. The documentation does not say why. This page counts them in the totals, shows them apart in the tables, and, where a trend depends on the ratings, tests what happens if all of them were strong (section 5).

Times are those of the sun. The SPC converts the time of a tornado to central standard time, whatever the state (37 tornadoes are on another clock). A tornado in Georgia at 17:00 central standard time struck at six in the evening by the clock there. To compare places, section 2 turns each time into the sun’s time at the place where the tornado began, from its longitude: an hour for every 15 degrees.

1. Where do tornadoes happen?

Code 
last_eight<-(last_year-7):last_year
us_a_year<-sum(tor$yr%in%last_eight)/length(last_eight)
ntp$Year<-as.integer(ntp$Year)
canada_tornadoes<-ntp[ntp$event_type%in%c("tornado_over_land","tornado_over_water")&
                      ntp$Year%in%last_eight,]
canada_a_year<-nrow(canada_tornadoes)/length(last_eight)
canada_water<-100*mean(canada_tornadoes$event_type=="tornado_over_water")
# the states since 2006, the years of the Enhanced Fujita scale: the tornadoes, those of EF2 and
# above and those of EF3 and above

More are reported, but the rise is mostly in the weak tornadoes. In 1950–1959 the SPC database had 479 tornadoes a year, in 2016–2025 1,318: 175% more, and a rank test of all the years finds the rise (the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend is less than 1 in 100). Much of the rise is in the weakest tornadoes: EF0 tornadoes went from 105 a year to 534. A study of the database found that the doubling of the count from the 1950s to the 2000s “is likely not related to meteorological causes alone”, and that the count of F1 and stronger tornadoes was steadier than that of F2 and stronger (Verbout et al. 2006); another says that changes in how tornadoes are reported “have made it difficult” to read the trend, and leaves out the weakest (Brooks et al. 2014). Counting from EF1 up, the rise is smaller: 374 a year at the start and 632 at the end (+69%), and the test does not clearly find a trend (6 in 100).

                 line=list(color=red,width=3),

                                      ": %{y:,.0f}<extra></extra>"),inherit=FALSE) %>%
    layout(xaxis=list(tick0=1950,dtick=20),yaxis=list(rangemode="tozero",tickformat=","))
  return(result)
}
p<-subplot(lapply(1:4,trend_panel),nrows=2,shareX=TRUE,margin=c(0.03,0.03,0.08,0.08))
# the title of each panel, above it
domains<-plotly_build(p)$x$layout
panel_titles<-lapply(1:4,function(k) {
  x_axis<-c("xaxis","xaxis2")[(k-1)%%2+1]
  y_axis<-c("yaxis","yaxis2","yaxis3","yaxis4")[k]
  list(text=paste0("<b>",panels[k],"</b>"),x=domains[[x_axis]]$domain[1],xref="paper",
       y=domains[[y_axis]]$domain[2],yref="paper",xanchor="left",yanchor="bottom",showarrow=FALSE)
})
p %>%
  chart("More tornadoes, or only more found?",
        paste0("NOAA Storm Prediction Center. Blue: the average of ",min(first_ten),"–",
               max(first_ten),"; red: of ",min(last_ten),"–",max(last_ten),
               ". Unrated tornadoes are in the first panel only."),
        annotations=panel_titles,showlegend=FALSE,margin=list(t=90,b=70),note_y=-0.1)

Interactive chart: More tornadoes, or only more found?

The strongest tornadoes are fewer, but be careful with that. The EF2 and stronger tornadoes fell from 189 a year to 142 (by chance less than 1 in 100), the EF3 and stronger from 50 to 28 (less than 1 in 100). Their peak year was 1973. But ratings are judgements of damage, they changed from one scale to the other in 2007, and from 2007 the unrated tornadoes grew in number, so this page does not conclude that the strong tornadoes have become rarer. The unrated tornadoes matter for the count of EF1 and above: if every one of them is counted in it, the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend becomes 1 in 100, against 6. For the years before 2007 alone it is 95 in 100, and for 2007 on 3 in 100. People killed fell from 142 a year to 51 (4 in 100); these data do not say why.

What changed more is how the tornadoes come. The days with at least one tornado of EF1 or above fell from 120.4 a year to 110.0, while the days with ten or more of them rose from 6.7 to 17.9 (the chances of the two patterns, less than 1 and less than 1 in 100). That is what a study of the database found, after setting aside the weakest tornadoes: the mean annual number “has remained relatively constant”, but the variability has increased since the 1970s, with fewer days with tornadoes and more days with many (Brooks et al. 2014).

So, what does it mean?

  1. A few states have the most tornadoes for their size, and they are not the largest. Mississippi, Alabama and Illinois had the most per area from 2006 to 2025, and Texas, the state with the most tornadoes, only 24th. Canada’s project finds about 112 a year, against 1,346 in the United States, but the two are not counted the same way.
  2. They come in the afternoon and evening, mostly in spring. 22% of them began in May, and each part of the country has its own busiest month.
  3. Most are weak and most deaths come from the strongest. EF4 and EF5 tornadoes were 0.9% of the tornadoes and 61% of the deaths.
  4. The worst years and days are far from the average. 27 April 2011 had 210 tornadoes in one day, and 2011 killed 553 people.
  5. More are counted, but that is not the same as more. The tornadoes of EF2 and above did not rise; what has changed is that the tornadoes of EF1 and above come on fewer days and in bigger groups.

What this does not show. There is no worldwide count: the data cover the United States and, in outline, Canada, and say nothing of the many countries where tornadoes are not systematically recorded, so this page cannot say that the United States has the most tornadoes in the world, only the most that are counted. Reports depend on who is there to see a tornado, and the ratings on what it destroyed. Averages by state hide the differences inside a state, and a rank test says whether a pattern is likely to be chance, not what causes it. And the counts say nothing of the people who live where tornadoes land.

For floods, see Floods; for all the hazards together, the overview.

item.title: Where the Water Rises: Large Floods in Every Part of the World
item.description: Where in the world floods happen, kill and displace the most people, when each part of the world floods, the worst floods on record, and whether floods have become more frequent or deadlier, from two open flood records.
item.content:encoded:
Where in the world floods happen, kill and displace the most people, when each part of the world floods, the worst floods on record, and whether floods have become more frequent or deadlier, from two open flood records.

What is this?

Wherever rain falls and a river runs, a flood is possible, so the records show floods in every part of the world. But they do not happen equally often, and they do not kill equally often. This story asks five questions:

  1. Where in the world do the large floods happen?
  2. Where do floods kill the most people?
  3. When does each part of the world flood?
  4. Which were the worst floods?
  5. Are floods more frequent or deadlier than they were?

It is one of a series on natural hazards: see Natural Disasters for the overview, and Tornadoes for another hazard of the weather.

No single record of floods is complete, so the page uses two, which count different things, and downloads them when it is rendered:

  • The Global Flood Records of the DFO Flood Observatory (University of Colorado), one row for each large flood from January 1985 to December 2023: when it started and ended, the countries it hit, its estimated cause, the people killed and the people displaced (DFO, data). DFO gives a flood an entry when it “appears to be large”: significant damage to buildings or farmland, a long time since the last similar flood, or deaths. It builds the record from news and government reports (DFO notes on the archive). The rows say where the flood was, not how many people lived there.
  • EM-DAT, the international disaster database of the Centre for Research on the Epidemiology of Disasters (CRED, UCLouvain), as yearly totals for each country since 2000: floods that are confirmed by at least two sources and meet one of its entry criteria, which are 10 or more deaths, 100 or more people affected, a call for international help or a declaration of an emergency (EM-DAT FAQ). The totals come from the Humanitarian Data Exchange.
  • The population and the land area of each country, and the continent it is in, from Our World in Data (population, land area, continents).

What counts as a flood. EM-DAT uses “flood” as a general term for water that overflows a river onto dry land, for higher-than-normal water along a coast or around a lake, and for flash floods, where water ponds where the rain fell; it includes glacial lake outburst floods (Our World in Data). Dead in EM-DAT means the dead plus the missing; in DFO, the missing are not counted. Affected in EM-DAT means injured, affected or homeless (EM-DAT). A tropical cyclone is a large storm that forms over warm sea and brings wind, heavy rain and a rise of the sea; a monsoon is a season of heavy rain that comes with a seasonal change in the wind.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("plotly", "jsonlite", "readxl"))
library(plotly)
library(jsonlite)
library(readxl)

The data

Code 
# a chart of Our World in Data as a table: one row for each country or region and each year
owid<-function(chart) {
  result<-read.csv(paste0("https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/",chart,
                          ".csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true"))

}

# the cause: written freely in the file (with typing mistakes and names of storms), sorted here by

cause_of<-function(x) {
  x<-tolower(x)
  result<-rep("Other or not given",length(x))
  result[grepl("rain|torrential",x)]<-"Heavy rain"
  result[grepl("snow|\\bice\\b|avalan",x)]<-"Snowmelt or ice"
  result[grepl("dam|levy|levee",x)]<-"Dam or levee failure"
  result[grepl("cyclone|tropical|typhoon|hurricane",x)]<-"Cyclone"
  result[grepl("monso|monoo",x)]<-"Monsoon rain"
  return(result)
}

The archive and the countries. The DFO archive has 5,503 records; 2 of them start in January 2024, after the end of the years it covers, and are left out. 424 records name more than one country, and a flood counts once for each country it hit. 18 records name only Czechoslovakia, Serbia Montenegro, Soviet Union and Yugoslavia, which no longer exist as countries, and are left out of the figures by country.

Tsunamis are not floods. DFO’s records have 5 tsunamis: 4 with the cause “tsunami”, and the record of 26 December 2004 in Thailand, which DFO calls a “tidal surge” and gives 160,000 dead: the date of the earthquake and tsunami in the Indian Ocean, which left 227,898 people dead or missing in all the countries on its shores (NOAA). EM-DAT counts the Thai tsunami with the earthquakes, with 8,345 dead and missing. These 5 are left out, which leaves 5,496 floods from 1985 to 2023.

EM-DAT: the years, and the empty cells. The yearly figures of EM-DAT that this page uses start in 2000, and they are those of the version of 25 November 2026. 2026 is not over, and its 61 floods so far are left out: the figures run from 2000 to 2025. In 24% of the rows of floods (a country, a year and a kind of flood) no number of dead is given, and in 6% no number of people affected. EM-DAT cannot tell an unreported number from none (EM-DAT FAQ), so a total here is a minimum, and the rows without a figure are counted as zero. A flood that hit several countries is a record in each. 5 rows for former countries are left out. EM-DAT includes 7 country-years of glacial lake outburst floods, which are kept.

1. Where in the world do the large floods happen?

Code 
# the groups: the continents, with Russia on its own
groups_all<-c("Africa","Asia","Europe without Russia","North America","Oceania","South America",
              "Russia")
# the floods of each group: a flood that hit two groups counts in both
in_groups<-unique(places_ok[,c("row","group")])
counts<-table(in_groups$group)
by_group<-data.frame(group=names(counts),n_floods=as.integer(counts))
group_land<-data.frame(code=country_codes,km2=land_of(country_codes),group=group_of(country_codes))
group_land<-aggregate(km2~group,data=group_land,FUN=sum)
by_group$km2<-group_land$km2[match(by_group$group,group_land$group)]
by_group$per_area<-by_group$n_floods/by_group$km2*1e6
by_group<-by_group[order(-by_group$n_floods),]
of_group<-function(g,column) {
  result<-by_group[[column]][by_group$group==g]
  return(result)
}
n_distinct_floods<-length(unique(places_ok$row))
# the countries, from the one with the most large floods
counts<-table(places_ok$code)
by_country<-data.frame(code=names(counts),n_floods=as.integer(counts))
by_country$name<-name_of(by_country$code)
by_country$km2<-land_of(by_country$code)
by_country$per_area<-by_country$n_floods/by_country$km2*1e6
by_country<-by_country[order(-by_country$n_floods),]
top_count<-head(by_country,5)
# per square kilometre, the countries of more than 25,000 square kilometres (the smallest ones
# would lead with a handful of floods)
min_km2<-25000
n_small<-sum(by_country$km2<min_km2,na.rm=TRUE)
large<-by_country[which(by_country$km2>=min_km2),]
top_area<-head(large[order(-large$per_area),],5)
in_country<-function(name,column) {
  result<-by_country[[column]][by_country$name==name]
  return(result)
}
# the share of the floods of each part of the world in the first three groups
share_asia<-100*of_group("Asia","n_floods")/n_distinct_floods
# a second record: the events that EM-DAT counts in each country from 2000 to the last year that
# both records have
both_from<-2000
both_to<-min(last_dfo_year,last_em_year)
in_years<-em_flood[em_flood$year>=both_from&em_flood$year<=both_to,]
em_count<-aggregate(cbind(n_em=events)~iso,data=in_years,FUN=sum)
names(em_count)[1]<-"code"
counts<-table(places_ok$code[places_ok$row%in%floods$row[floods$year>=both_from]])
dfo_count<-data.frame(code=names(counts),n_dfo=as.integer(counts))
top_em<-head(em_count$code[order(-em_count$n_em)],10)
top_dfo<-head(dfo_count$code[order(-dfo_count$n_dfo)],10)
shared_top<-intersect(top_em,top_dfo)
only_em<-setdiff(top_em,top_dfo)
only_dfo<-setdiff(top_dfo,top_em)
europe<-places_ok[places_ok$group%in%c("Europe without Russia"),]
n_europe<-length(unique(europe$row))
greece_n<-sum(places_ok$code=="GRC")
greece_years<-aggregate(dead~year,data=em_flood[em_flood$iso=="GRC",],FUN=sum,na.rm=TRUE,
                        na.action=na.pass)
greece_worst<-greece_years[which.max(greece_years$dead),]

Asia: more than two in five of the large floods. DFO’s 5,496 large floods from 1985 to 2023 include 5,479 in at least one country that has a continent (a flood that crosses a border counts in each continent it touches). 43% of these floods were in Asia: 2,361 floods, one for every 13,160 square kilometres of land. In South America there were 501, in North America 886, in Africa 913, in Europe without Russia 481, in Oceania 249 and in Russia 115. Per square kilometre, Europe without Russia has 2.7 times as many large floods as Africa does, which may say as much about how much news reaches DFO as about floods: its notes say that news from poorer countries tends to arrive later and in less detail (DFO notes on the archive).

Code 
bars<-by_group[order(by_group$n_floods),] # the largest at the top
bars$group<-factor(bars$group,levels=bars$group)
bar_colors<-ifelse(bars$group=="Asia",red,gray)
left<-plot_ly(bars,x=~n_floods,y=~group,type="bar",orientation="h",marker=list(color=bar_colors),

series$panel<-factor(series$panel,levels=panels)
# one panel: a series by year, and its year with the most in red, with its value
trend_panel<-function(x) {
  top<-x[x$value==max(x$value),]
  result<-plot_ly(x,x=~year,y=~value,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers",
                  line=list(color=dark_gray,width=1),marker=list(color=dark_gray,size=5),
                  hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:,}<extra></extra>") %>%
    add_trace(data=top,x=~year,y=~value,type="scatter",mode="markers+text",
              marker=list(color=red,size=10),text=~paste(year,"·",number(value)),
              textposition="middle right",hoverinfo="skip",inherit=FALSE)
  return(result)
}
p<-subplot(lapply(split(series,series$panel),trend_panel),nrows=3,shareX=TRUE,margin=0.06)
# the title of each panel, above it
domains<-plotly_build(p)$x$layout
panel_titles<-lapply(1:3,function(k) {
  list(text=paste0("<b>",panels[k],"</b>"),x=0,xref="paper",
       y=domains[[c("yaxis","yaxis2","yaxis3")[k]]]$domain[2],yref="paper",xanchor="left",
       yanchor="bottom",showarrow=FALSE)
})
values_axis<-list(rangemode="tozero",tickformat=",")
p %>%
  chart("More floods, or more reporting?",
        paste0("DFO Global Flood Records v0.9.0; EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain, ",
               "via the Humanitarian Data Exchange. Red: the year with the most."),
        x_axis=list(range=c(first_dfo_year-1,last_dfo_year+8),tick0=1990,dtick=10),
        y_axis=values_axis,yaxis2=values_axis,yaxis3=values_axis,annotations=panel_titles,
        showlegend=FALSE,margin=list(t=80,b=70),note_y=-0.08)

Interactive chart: More floods, or more reporting?

So, what does it mean?

  1. Asia has the most large floods. 43% of the large floods of the record, and the countries with the most are the United States, China and India. Per square kilometre, Haiti and Sri Lanka lead.
  2. A few large countries have most of the dead, and other countries have the most for each person. The ten countries with the most dead have 63% of the deaths in EM-DAT since 2000; per million people, Haiti leads, with 12.6 a year.
  3. Every part of the world has its wet season. Asia floods in June to September, South America and Oceania in the first months of the year.
  4. A few floods kill most of the people. The 10 deadliest floods have 60% of the dead of DFO’s floods, and 5 of them came with a cyclone.
  5. The records do not show a clear rise in floods or in flood deaths since 2000. Older counts rise and fall with the way floods were recorded.

What this does not show. Neither record is a count of all floods: DFO records the large floods that the news and government reports tell of, and EM-DAT those that meet its entry criteria, so a country with little news coverage or few reports may have more floods than it shows. A flood that kills nobody, in a country that does not ask for help, may appear in neither. The counts are of floods, not of how long they lasted or how much land they covered, and the estimates of the dead, the missing and the displaced differ between sources. Nothing here says what causes floods, or whether climate change is changing them: for that, a record must be built to measure it. And the table of the worst floods leaves out the records that did not agree with the other source, which may include a true record that EM-DAT lists differently.

For the overview of all the hazards, see Natural Disasters; for another hazard of the weather, Tornadoes; for the fire that follows the dry season, Where the World Burns.

EM-DAT is free for non-commercial use under its Database License Agreement and is not open data; the country profiles are published under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, and this page shows totals and counts worked out from them, not the data.
