item.title: Where the Earth Shakes: Earthquakes Around the World Since 1900
item.description: Earthquakes in the USGS catalogue: where in the world they strike, how often and how strong, how deep, the deadliest, and whether there are more of them than there used to be.
item.content:encoded:
Earthquakes in the USGS catalogue: where in the world they strike, how often and how strong, how deep, the deadliest, and whether there are more of them than there used to be.

What is this?

An earthquake comes without warning, and the strongest can wreck a city in a minute. This story asks where they strike, and four more questions:

  1. Where in the world do the earthquakes strike?
  2. How often, and how strong?
  3. How deep are they?
  4. Which were the deadliest?
  5. Are there more of them than there used to be?

For the other hazards of the series, see Tsunamis, Volcanoes and the overview of natural disasters.

The data come from three places, downloaded when the page is rendered:

  • The earthquakes: the catalogue of the United States Geological Survey (USGS), called ComCat, which collects the earthquakes that seismic networks around the world report: the date, the place, the magnitude and the depth (ComCat, queried through its web service). The page uses every earthquake of magnitude 6 and above since 1900, and every one of magnitude 5 and above since 1973.
  • The deaths: the Significant Earthquake Database of the US National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI, part of NOAA), which lists destructive earthquakes with the number of people they killed (NCEI). The USGS catalogue has no deaths.
  • The map: the boundaries of the tectonic plates, from Peter Bird’s digital model (Bird 2003) in the version of Hugo Ahlenius and Nordpil (tectonicplates), and the outlines of the countries, from Natural Earth.

The magnitude is the size of the earthquake. Each whole number up is a tenfold increase in the ground motion that a seismograph records and 32 times more energy released (USGS). So a magnitude 7 earthquake releases 32 times the energy of a magnitude 6, and about a thousand times (32 × 32) that of a magnitude 5. This page writes magnitude 6 as M6, and “M6+” for magnitude 6 and above.

The depth is how far below the surface the rock starts to break, in kilometres. The USGS calls an earthquake shallow when it is between 0 and 70 km deep, intermediate between 70 and 300 km and deep between 300 and 700 km (USGS).

The tectonic plates are the large slabs that make up the outer shell of the Earth. They move against each other, and the earthquakes are not spread evenly: look at where the plates meet.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("plotly", "sf", "jsonlite"))
library(plotly)
library(sf)
library(jsonlite)

The data

Code 
# only complete years: from 1 January of this year, the catalogue is incomplete
last_year<-as.integer(format(Sys.Date(),"%Y"))-1
# the USGS catalogue as a table: the earthquakes between two dates, of at least a magnitude
# (a query returns 20,000 earthquakes at most, so the magnitude 5 and above come in pieces)
usgs<-function(from,to,magnitude) {
  result<-read.csv(paste0("https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/query?format=csv",
                          "&starttime=",from,"-01-01&endtime=",to,"-01-01","&minmagnitude=",
                          magnitude,"&orderby=time-asc&limit=20000"))
  return(result)
}
# magnitude 6 and above, since 1900
big<-usgs(1900,last_year+1,6)
# magnitude 5 and above, since 1973, eight years at a time
starts<-seq(1973,last_year,by=8)
ends<-c(starts[-1],last_year+1)
middle<-do.call(rbind,Map(function(a,b) usgs(a,b,5),starts,ends))
# the destructive earthquakes of NCEI, with deaths, since 1900, 200 to a page
noaa_url<-paste0("https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/hazel/hazard-service/api/v1/earthquakes",
                 "?minYear=1900&minDeaths=1")
first_page<-fromJSON(noaa_url)
deadly<-do.call(rbind,lapply(seq_len(first_page$totalPages),function(i) {
  fromJSON(paste0(noaa_url,"&page=",i))$items[,c("year","locationName","country","eqMagnitude",
                                                 "deaths","deathsTotal","latitude","longitude")]
}))
# the plate boundaries (Bird 2003), and the countries (Natural Earth, 1:50 million)
plates<-st_read(paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fraxen/tectonicplates/master/",
                       "GeoJSON/PB2002_boundaries.json"),quiet=TRUE)
land<-st_read(paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvkelso/natural-earth-vector/master/",
                     "geojson/ne_50m_admin_0_countries.geojson"),quiet=TRUE)
land<-land[,c("NAME_LONG","ADM0_A3","CONTINENT")]
Code 
red<-"#d62728"
gray<-"#bdbdbd"
dark_gray<-"#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes
# the three depths, in order, whose neighbours were checked for colour blindness
depth_colors<-c(Shallow="#d97706",Intermediate="#be123c",Deep="#5b3fb5")
# one hue, from light to dark, for amounts: the map of the countries
blues<-c("#eff3ff","#c6dbef","#9ecae1","#6baed6","#3182bd","#08519c","#08306b")
# the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(),
                margin=list(t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.16,...) {
  note<-list(text=paste("Source:",source),xref="paper",yref="paper",x=0,y=note_y,xanchor="left",
             yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=11,color=dark_gray))
  result<-layout(p,title=list(text=title,x=0.02,xanchor="left",y=0.97,yanchor="top"),
                 yaxis=c(list(title=y_title),y_axis),xaxis=c(list(title=""),x_axis),margin=margin,
                 annotations=c(annotations,list(note)),...) %>%
    config(displaylogo=FALSE)
  return(result)
}
legend_top<-list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.02,yanchor="bottom")
# numbers in the text
number<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x),big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE,trim=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
percent<-function(x,digits=0) {
  result<-paste0(format(round(x,digits),nsmall=digits,trim=TRUE),"%")
  return(result)
}
one<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x,1),nsmall=1,trim=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
two<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x,2),nsmall=2,trim=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
and_list<-function(x) {
  if(length(x)<2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  result<-paste(paste(head(x,-1),collapse=", "),"and",tail(x,1))
  return(result)
}
# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one
# without a trend
chance<-function(x,years) {
  p<-cor.test(years,x,method="kendall",exact=FALSE)$p.value
  result<-if(p<0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100*p))
  return(result)
}
# the distance in kilometres between two points (longitude and latitude in degrees)
distance_km<-function(lon1,lat1,lon2,lat2) {
  r<-pi/180
  h<-sin((lat2-lat1)*r/2)^2+cos(lat1*r)*cos(lat2*r)*sin((lon2-lon1)*r/2)^2
  result<-12742*asin(sqrt(h))
  return(result)
}
Code 
# only earthquakes: the catalogue also holds explosions, and more
all_types<-table(c(big$type,middle$type))
n_blasts<-sum(all_types[names(all_types)=="nuclear explosion"])
n_other<-sum(all_types[!names(all_types)%in%c("earthquake","nuclear explosion")])
quakes<-function(x) {
  x<-x[x$type=="earthquake",]
  x$year<-as.integer(substr(x$time,1,4))
  return(x)
}
n_before<-nrow(big)+nrow(middle)
big<-quakes(big)
middle<-quakes(middle)
magnitude_types<-sort(table(middle$magType),decreasing=TRUE)
# the depth classes of the USGS
depth_class<-function(depth) {
  result<-cut(depth,c(-Inf,70,300,Inf),labels=names(depth_colors),right=FALSE)
  return(result)
}
middle$depth_class<-depth_class(middle$depth)
big$depth_class<-depth_class(big$depth)
# depths that a location program sets when the data do not fix the depth (USGS: 10 and 33 km)
fixed_depth<-mean(middle$depth%in%c(10,33))
other_depth<-max(table(middle$depth[!middle$depth%in%c(10,33)]))/nrow(middle)
above_sea<-sum(middle$depth<0)
# each earthquake of magnitude 5 and above: the country it is in; or the nearest country, if the
# sea is less than 200 km wide between the two; or nowhere. Planar geometry on longitude and
# latitude is accurate enough to find the nearest country; the distance itself is then worked out
# on the globe.
sf_use_s2(FALSE)
points<-st_as_sf(middle[,c("id","longitude","latitude")],coords=c("longitude","latitude"),crs=4326)
inside<-st_intersects(points,land)
on_land<-lengths(inside)>0
nearest<-st_nearest_feature(points[!on_land,],land)
lines<-st_nearest_points(points[!on_land,],land[nearest,],pairwise=TRUE)
ends_xy<-st_coordinates(st_cast(lines,"POINT"))
from_xy<-ends_xy[seq(1,nrow(ends_xy),by=2),]
to_xy<-ends_xy[seq(2,nrow(ends_xy),by=2),]
offshore_km<-distance_km(from_xy[,1],from_xy[,2],to_xy[,1],to_xy[,2])
middle$place_index<-NA_integer_
middle$place_index[on_land]<-vapply(inside[on_land],`[`,1L,1L)
reach<-200
middle$place_index[!on_land][offshore_km<=reach]<-nearest[offshore_km<=reach]
land$NAME_LONG[land$NAME_LONG=="Russian Federation"]<-"Russia"
land$NAME_LONG[land$NAME_LONG=="South Georgia and the Islands"]<-"South Georgia"
middle$country<-land$NAME_LONG[middle$place_index]
middle$code<-land$ADM0_A3[middle$place_index]
middle$continent<-land$CONTINENT[middle$place_index]
# each earthquake of magnitude 6 and above since 1973: its distance from the nearest plate boundary
big_now<-big[big$year>=1973,]
points_now<-st_as_sf(big_now[,c("id","longitude","latitude")],coords=c("longitude","latitude"),
                     crs=4326)
near_boundary<-st_nearest_feature(points_now,plates)
lines_now<-st_nearest_points(points_now,plates[near_boundary,],pairwise=TRUE)
xy_now<-st_coordinates(st_cast(lines_now,"POINT"))
from_now<-xy_now[seq(1,nrow(xy_now),by=2),]
to_now<-xy_now[seq(2,nrow(xy_now),by=2),]
big_now$boundary_km<-distance_km(from_now[,1],from_now[,2],to_now[,1],to_now[,2])
# the same distance for points spread evenly over the globe: how much of the world is near a
# boundary
set.seed(2026)
n_random<-4000
random_points<-st_as_sf(data.frame(lon=runif(n_random,-180,180),
                                   lat=asin(runif(n_random,-1,1))*180/pi),
                        coords=c("lon","lat"),crs=4326)
near_random<-st_nearest_feature(random_points,plates)
lines_random<-st_cast(st_nearest_points(random_points,plates[near_random,],pairwise=TRUE),"POINT")
xy_random<-st_coordinates(lines_random)
from_random<-xy_random[seq(1,nrow(xy_random),by=2),]
to_random<-xy_random[seq(2,nrow(xy_random),by=2),]
random_km<-distance_km(from_random[,1],from_random[,2],to_random[,1],to_random[,2])
sf_use_s2(TRUE)
# the deaths: the NCEI total where it has one
deadly$deaths_all<-ifelse(is.na(deadly$deathsTotal),deadly$deaths,deadly$deathsTotal)
deadly<-deadly[!is.na(deadly$deaths_all)&deadly$year<=last_year,]
deadly$name<-ifelse(deadly$country=="USA","United States",
                    tools::toTitleCase(tolower(deadly$country)))
# the place as NCEI writes it, in words: the parts between colons, without compass points
place_text<-function(x) {
  parts<-strsplit(tolower(x),"\\s*:\\s*")
  result<-vapply(parts,function(p) {
    p<-trimws(p)
    paste(tools::toTitleCase(p[!p%in%c("n","s","e","w","ne","nw","se","sw","")]),collapse=", ")
  },"")
  return(result)
}
deadly$place<-place_text(deadly$locationName)

Only earthquakes. The catalogue also holds explosions, mine collapses and landslides. Of the 102,788 events that the two downloads found, 494 were nuclear explosions and 69 were other things (an explosion, a rock burst, a volcanic eruption and so on). The page uses the other 102,225, labelled earthquakes. 14,358 of them are magnitude 6 and above since 1900 and 87,867 magnitude 5 and above since 1973, and the second group includes most of the first from 1973 on.

Only whole years. The page stops at the end of 2025, so that every year counts in full.

Many magnitudes. The catalogue gives each earthquake the magnitude that its source chose, of several kinds: from 1973 on, 47% of the magnitude 5 and above are of the kind called mb, and the others are of kinds such as Mw (the moment magnitude, the one that scientists prefer for large earthquakes). Section 5 shows what that means for counting earthquakes over the years.

Which country? The catalogue’s place is a piece of text, not a country code, so each earthquake of magnitude 5 and above is placed on the map of the countries. Only 20% fall inside a country: the rest happen under the sea. An earthquake at sea is given to the nearest country when it is within 200 km of its coast (56% of all of them); the other 24%, in the open sea, belong to no country. Countries are those of Natural Earth, which counts overseas territories (Puerto Rico, Guam) as places of their own, and a country’s earthquakes are the ones under it and near it.

The depth is the least certain number. It is the least constrained of all the parameters of an earthquake, says the USGS, and where the data do not fix it, the location program sets a default, often 10 or 33 km (ComCat). 40% of the magnitude 5 and above have exactly 10 or 33 km (the next most common depth has 3%), so the depths on this page are good for classes (shallow, intermediate, deep) and not for the exact kilometre. 27 of them are negative, which means above the reference level that the source used.

1. Where in the world do the earthquakes strike?

Code 
n_big<-nrow(big_now)
within<-function(km) {
  result<-percent(100*mean(big_now$boundary_km<=km))
  return(result)
}
world_within<-function(km) {
  result<-percent(100*mean(random_km<=km))
  return(result)
}
# the earthquakes of each country, the most first (a key of the three columns keeps a missing code)
on_land<-middle[!is.na(middle$country),]
keys<-paste(on_land$country,on_land$code,on_land$continent,sep="|")
places<-do.call(rbind,lapply(split(on_land,keys),function(x) {
  data.frame(country=x$country[1],
             code=x$code[1],
             continent=x$continent[1],
             n=nrow(x),
             strong=sum(x$mag>=6))
}))
places<-places[order(-places$n,places$country,method="radix"),]
rownames(places)<-NULL
n_years<-last_year-1973+1
n_places<-nrow(places)
top<-head(places,15)
sea_share<-100*mean(is.na(middle$country))
place_of<-function(name,column) {
  result<-places[[column]][places$country==name]
  return(result)
}
rank_of<-function(name) {
  result<-match(name,places$country)
  return(result)
}
# Europe: the continent of Natural Earth, without Russia (most of its earthquakes are in Kamchatka
# and the Kuril Islands, in the east) and with Turkey, which Natural Earth puts in Asia, counted
# on its own
europe<-head(places[which(places$continent=="Europe"&places$country!="Russia"),],4)

Along narrow belts, and mostly under the sea. The 7,327 earthquakes of magnitude 6 and above from 1973 to 2025 do not fall at random: 65% of them are within 100 km of a plate boundary and 92% within 300 km. Of the surface of the globe, only 10% is within 100 km of a boundary and 24% within 300 km (worked out for 4,000 points spread evenly over the globe). Where plates meet, one slides under the other, or they grind side by side, and the rock breaks.

Code 
# the plate boundaries as one line with gaps
coords<-as.data.frame(st_coordinates(plates))
gaps<-do.call(rbind,lapply(split(coords[,c("X","Y")],coords$L1),function(x) {
  rbind(x,data.frame(X=NA,Y=NA))
}))
shown<-big_now
shown$text<-paste0("M",format(shown$mag,nsmall=1),", ",shown$year,", ",round(shown$depth),
                   " km deep")
p<-plot_ly() %>%
  add_trace(type="scattergeo",mode="lines",lon=round(gaps$X,2),lat=round(gaps$Y,2),
            line=list(color=dark_gray,width=0.8),name="Plate boundaries",hoverinfo="skip")
depth_ranges<-c(Shallow="under 70 km",Intermediate="70–300 km",Deep="300 km or more")
for(k in names(depth_colors)) {
  x<-shown[shown$depth_class==k,]
  p<-add_trace(p,type="scattergeo",mode="markers",lon=x$longitude,lat=x$latitude,text=x$text,
               hoverinfo="text",name=paste0(k," (",depth_ranges[[k]],")"),
               marker=list(color=depth_colors[[k]],size=4.5,opacity=0.75,line=list(width=0)))
}
p %>%
  chart(paste0("Earthquakes of magnitude 6 and above, 1973–",last_year),
        paste0("USGS ComCat; plate boundaries: Bird (2003), ",
               "via Ahlenius/Nordpil; countries: Natural Earth."),
        geo=list(showframe=FALSE,showcoastlines=TRUE,coastlinecolor="#cccccc",showland=TRUE,
                 landcolor="#f0f0f0",projection=list(type="natural earth"),
                 lataxis=list(range=c(-65,85))),
        legend=list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.0,yanchor="bottom"),margin=list(t=80,b=40,l=0,r=0),
        note_y=-0.02)

Interactive chart: Earthquakes of magnitude 6 and above, 1973–2025

Indonesia leads, then Papua New Guinea and Japan. Counting every earthquake of magnitude 5 and above from 1973 to 2025 under a country or within 200 km of its coast, Indonesia had 11,920, Papua New Guinea 5,488 and Japan 5,093: 224.9, 103.5 and 96.1 a year. 24% of all the earthquakes of this size were farther than 200 km from any country.

Code

bars$country<-factor(bars$country,levels=bars$country)
plot_ly(bars,x=~n,y=~country,type="bar",orientation="h",
        marker=list(color=ifelse(bars$strong==max(bars$strong),red,gray)),text=~number(n),
        textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE,

        note_y=-0.1)

Interactive chart: Most earthquakes of magnitude 5+, 1973–2025

}))
plot_ly(on_map,type="choropleth",locations=~code,z=~class,zmin=0.5,zmax=6.5,colorscale=steps,
        marker=list(line=list(color="white",width=0.3)),
        text=~paste0(country,": ",number(n)," earthquakes of magnitude 5+<br>",strong,
                     " of magnitude 6+"),
        hoverinfo="text",
        colorbar=list(title=list(text="Earthquakes of magnitude 5+",side="top"),orientation="h",
                      x=0.5,xanchor="center",y=-0.02,yanchor="top",tickvals=1:6,
                      ticktext=class_names,len=0.95,thickness=14,tickangle=0,
                      tickfont=list(size=10))) %>%
  chart(paste0("Earthquakes of magnitude 5+ by country, ",1973,"–",last_year),
        paste0("USGS ComCat; countries: Natural Earth. ",
               "Under the country or within 200 km of its coast. Grey: none."),
        geo=list(showframe=FALSE,showcoastlines=FALSE,showland=TRUE,landcolor="#e8e8e8",
                 projection=list(type="natural earth"),lataxis=list(range=c(-57,85))),
        margin=list(t=50,b=130,l=0,r=0),note_y=-0.27)

Interactive chart: Earthquakes of magnitude 5+ by country, 1973–2025

No clear trend in the big ones; the smaller ones are counted in steps. Earthquakes of magnitude 7 and above are the only ones that the catalogue seems to record in full since 1900 (see below). They averaged 12.4 a year from 1900 to 1949, 11.1 from 1950 to 1989 and 15.0 from 1990 to 2025: not a steady rise. From 1990 on, a rank test finds no trend in them (the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend is 64 in 100). Over all the years from 1900 the test leans slightly upwards (3 in 100), because of the dip in the middle of the century; the page does not take that for a lasting rise, since magnitudes were worked out differently in each period.

For the smaller earthquakes the catalogue is the problem, not the Earth. From 1900 to 1904 it holds 15.4 earthquakes of magnitude 6 and above a year, and from 1905 to 1914 55.8; for magnitude 7 and above the same years give 12.0 and 15.7, so only the strongest were recorded in those years. Even from 1973 the counts of magnitude 6 and above are not on one level: they average 93.1 a year before 1983 and 148.7 from 1983 on, a step of 60%. So, what does it mean?

  1. Earthquakes come in belts. 65% of the 7,327 of magnitude 6 and above since 1973 struck within 100 km of a plate boundary, which is near only 10% of the surface of the globe. 24% of those of magnitude 5 and above were farther than 200 km from any country.
  2. Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and Japan have the most. Greece is number 22 among 172 countries and territories, and the first in Europe without Russia.
  3. There are about 0.9 earthquakes of magnitude 8 a year and about 14 of magnitude 7, and each step down in magnitude is several times as common.
  4. Nearly all are shallow, 79% of those of magnitude 5 and above. The deaths come in a few events: the ten deadliest earthquakes killed 61% of the 2,531,015 recorded since 1900.
  5. There is no clear sign of more earthquakes in this catalogue. From 1990 on there is no trend in those of magnitude 7 and above; the smaller ones are counted in steps, and the page does not claim a trend for them.

What this does not show. The catalogue is of the earthquakes that instruments record, and the earlier years of it are patchy for all but the strongest. The magnitude is of several kinds, and the depth is uncertain. The countries come from the places of the earthquakes, not from where the shaking was felt. The deaths are those NCEI recorded for its significant earthquakes: some counts are estimates, and the tsunamis that follow some earthquakes are not told apart here. And earthquakes of the same size do not do the same harm.
